the commission's vice-president mr president, the community's competence to take the necessary measures to combat discrimination, and in particular discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, is based on article 13 of the ec treaty. the commission also recalls that the prohibition of such discrimination is explicitly enshrined in article 21 of the charter of fundamental rights. on this basis, the commission, within the framework of its powers, is and will be making every effort to combat homophobia firmly. combating discrimination based on sexual orientation is an essential element in the fight against homophobia. directive 2000/78/ec establishing a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation, which covers all types of discrimination referred to in article 13, is a concrete example of this action and the commission is monitoring and will monitor the implementation of this directive in the member states. the commission is nevertheless aware that legislative action must be accompanied by other initiatives to combat de facto discrimination, humiliating practices, prejudice and stereotypes. let me mention two specific actions undertaken by the commission: the first action is an information campaign, launched in 2003, entitled 'for diversity against discrimination', which is currently underway and aims to promote a positive image of diversity and to inform the public about anti-discrimination laws. gay rights organisations are among the partners in this action and several initiatives have been undertaken, such as an information campaign and raising public awareness of the discrimination suffered by gay people. the second initiative is part of the recent proposal to make 2007 the european year of equal opportunities for all. the objectives will be to inform the public of their rights, to promote diversity as an asset and an opportunity for the union, and to promote equal opportunities for all, whether in economic, social, cultural or political life. the commission considers that organisations fighting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation will be able to benefit greatly from the latter action. the fact remains that the union and the commission can only act within the limits of the powers conferred on them by the treaty. for example, the commission may initiate possible infringement proceedings against a member state, but only if a violation of fundamental rights is found in the context of the application of community law. but beyond the union's competence, it is the responsibility of the member states to take the necessary measures to combat homophobia. in any event, whether the situations are within or outside the framework of community law, it is clear that the commission absolutely condemns any manifestation or expression of homophobia.

the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank mr el khadraoui and mr zīle very warmly for their work and for the spirit of cooperation which has guided our work. i also thank the members of the committee on transport and tourism for their commitment to this important debate. i would point out, mr president, that this debate is timely, even though i have to prepare new air agreements during the course of 2006. it was very desirable that parliament should inform me of the community's external policy in the field of air transport. these two reports are indeed an important contribution to the interinstitutional dialogue on community action in this field. the community has, over the last 20 years, seen its responsibilities in the air transport sector increase. member states have removed the boundaries of their national markets to form a single market - the community market - which is now based on a comprehensive set of common rules, including in areas such as safety, security or air traffic management. this community of law forms the basis of a market which has grown in importance over the years. we now have 600 million passengers and 60 million tonnes of goods carried annually. the transition from a bilateral approach between states to agreements negotiated at community level offers new and considerable prospects thanks to the opportunities offered by the large european market and the community's possibilities for cooperation. it is also this shift from a bilateral to a community approach which is a legal necessity for our regulatory acquis in the air transport sector to be recognised and respected. mr el khadraoui's report deals with a number of key problems in our policy. firstly, the importance of moving towards the regularisation of bilateral agreements which, since the court's judgments, have been subject to legal uncertainty. mr el khadraoui, we are engaged in this task alongside the member states, in a spirit of close cooperation and using all the levers offered by the european union's external policy. secondly, you have stressed, and i thank you for this, the need to always respect this dual objective: opening up markets, regulatory convergence. this priority given to regulatory convergence allows us to develop our international activities and the international activities of our industry, in conditions of fair and healthy competition. we must pursue these two paths inseparably. this is a guarantee of the community's effectiveness and credibility in the negotiations. finally, this regulatory cooperation should be based as much as possible on technical cooperation to ensure a high level of convergence in such crucial areas as safety and security. but also, of course, in the environmental and social problems which are part of our european social model. with parliament's support, we will continue to ask for new negotiating mandates. the integration of ukraine into the european area, an agreement with australia and chile, the launch of negotiations with china and india - these will be the priorities for 2006. china and russia are the subject of two commission communications on which mr zīle's report is based. i shall begin with russia and the question of the flyover of siberia. i thank you for your support on this matter and for your very justified demand. we are determined to put an end to these tax levies which are clearly outside all international rules and before we consider a comprehensive air agreement with russia we must resolve this specific issue also taking into account russia's wish to join the wto. i've been stepping up the pace of negotiations with the russian government over the last few months. the issue was raised at the eu-russia summit in october following a letter from president barroso to president putin. i have had two meetings with the russian minister for transport, mr igor levitin, during which i have stressed the urgency of a solution. we are very firm in our position, we are asking the russian government to establish a transparent and non-discriminatory system and to gradually reduce levies until 2013, the date agreed in 2004 between the russian government and the commission. finally, we call for the abolition of quantitative restrictions on european airlines flying over siberia. if the russian government does not react sufficiently at this stage, we must bring this matter up again at all levels. this issue must be resolved before russia joins the wto. as regards china, a growing market, the advantages of a community approach are clear, as mr zīle has shown. the prospect of an agreement with china is essential for european operators in the long term. but our approach to china must be gradual and orderly, in order to strengthen our cooperation while developing a level of regulatory convergence acceptable to our industry. the first phase of negotiations must necessarily be devoted to improving the regulatory framework and the conditions for commercial exploitation. our companies are suffering from unjustified restrictions that must be lifted immediately. these aspects of doing business will be our priority. in any case, mr president, i should like to thank the european parliament very much for its contribution to the success of this great negotiation which will enable the european union to expand the possibilities of its air transport industry, an industry which, i believe, has had the merit of creating jobs in europe and of showing us the face of a particularly dynamic europe and a europe where the development of transport is accompanied by a high level of safety and a high quality of transport. i would like to thank mr el khadraoui, mr zīle and your committee once again.

the president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the events of the first week of january in connection with the gas dispute between the russian federation and ukraine have made it very clear to us that we cannot take security of energy supply for granted. more than a quarter of the european union's gas consumption is covered by imports from russia. up to 80% of these are transported via ukraine. therefore, the uninterrupted and continuous transport of gas from russia through ukraine to the european union is essential for households and businesses. in fact, however, some eu member states experienced delivery failures of up to 50% on 1 and 2 january this year. the european commission and the austrian presidency have taken a diplomatic initiative to help bring these failures to a speedy end. in this context, i would also like to address the problems between moldova and russia and ask both partners to seek a longer-term solution at the negotiating table. according to media reports, there's an agreement for a three-month period. but that's certainly very short-term. now it is time to learn the right lessons from the events. in my view, the following three measures are necessary to ensure the long-term security of europe's natural gas supply: first, diversification of sources and transport routes for natural gas. a number of new pipeline projects with a total transport capacity of 140 billion m3 per year are being planned. these projects must be implemented quickly. the nabucco pipeline from austria to the caspian sea via turkey is a promising project. this 3 300 km gas pipeline could, at the final stage of construction around 2020, transport up to 31 billion m3 of natural gas on a new route to the european union. secondly, the promotion of the use of liquefied natural gas (lng). the current capacity of existing plants is about 60 billion m3 per year. in some countries, projects are under way to build new terminals or to extend existing facilities. by 2010, capacity can be expected to increase to 160 billion m3 per year. the european union should aim to increase imported lng volumes by fivefold by 2010. this will also open up other supply regions to the european union, which cannot be connected by pipeline. thirdly, increased transparency in the hydrocarbon markets in order to reduce the high price volatility and to ensure stable, market-reflecting prices and better information on imported natural gas volumes. the key to this is considerable investment. in order to ensure that companies are prepared to make these investments, it is essential to create the most favourable investment climate possible in the energy sector. in the short term, we will have to think about how to avoid similar situations or how to overcome them without consequences. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the electricity supply. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation of the gas industry in the community. the increase in the intra-community exchange of gas naturally requires the availability of the necessary gas volumes, which is why we must also make efforts to support the establishment of liquid wholesale markets. another instrument in the short term is certainly the maintenance of gas stocks to bridge two-month supply gaps, taking into account national specificities such as storage in geological cavities or storage at power plants or industrial plants. the austrian presidency will focus on energy policy and in particular on the security of energy supplies. security of supply is one of the three pillars, along with competitiveness and, of course, sustainability of european energy policy, at national and community level. europe needs to do more to meet the energy challenges: globally, we're going to have 50% more energy consumption by 2030. europe's dependence on fossil fuel imports will increase significantly. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. within the european community we will have to increase the diversification of energy supply through increased use of renewable energy sources, for example by tripling the use of biomass by 2010. the cost-effective use of renewable energy sources is to become a mainstay of europe's energy supply. the use of clean coal and, in the long term, the use of hydrogen will also be an option for europe. from the austrian point of view, however, the use of nuclear energy is not an option. overall, it will be necessary on the supply side to continue the efforts towards a common european internal market and to increase investment in energy supply. on the consumer side, it will be necessary to improve energy efficiency in the community. there are currently large differences between member states in energy efficiency, measured as energy consumption per unit of gross domestic product. in this context, we can jointly refer to the agreement reached by the european parliament and the council on the directive on energy end-use efficiency and energy services. the events of new year's day have also shown the importance of the european union's relations with its partners. these partnerships should be pursued consistently at multilateral level for example through dialogues in the international energy forum or in the framework of the energy treaty with south-eastern europe and at bilateral level in the framework of the european union-russia or european union-opec dialogue . the willingness to cooperate is a very important element in securing energy supplies. so we have a wealth of options. it is up to us to use them effectively and quickly. as a secure energy future for the european union is in the interest of all member states, i am convinced that we will succeed. (applause from the centre)
member of the commission. mr president, i should like to thank parliament for finding time today to debate the security of energy supplies and particularly gas. in a way, it is a continuation of the debate we had on high oil prices last year. the current price of oil is more than usd 60 per barrel. the gas dispute between ukraine and russia triggered the debate on the security of supply to the european union. the gas dispute hit the headlines at the beginning of this year when russia stopped its supply to ukraine for a day and a half. that also had an impact on the eu through a reduction in the amount of gas reaching the european union. while it is reassuring in the short term that an agreement was reached between ukraine and russia, we must be under no illusions. the issue has not gone away. commercial negotiations between the two sides will continue in order to find a price adjustment formula that is mutually acceptable. we have also seen the repercussions internally in ukraine, with the vote of no confidence in the government last week. nor must we forget that the gas price dispute between russia and moldova was resolved only yesterday, with more detailed negotiations in the near future. i firmly believe that everyone needs to learn the lessons from the events at the beginning of the year. so, what are the lessons the eu should draw from this dispute? firstly, in the context of this particular dispute, the eu was, and should be, proactive. we not only maintained close bilateral contacts with both parties throughout the dispute but also urged them to resolve this dispute. while it is evident that the eu could not and should not take sides, we made it clear to both sides that it was in their strong interest to come to an agreement rapidly. in such a situation it is very important to have close cooperation between the council – in particular the presidency – and the commission. secondly, the dispute has underlined the usefulness of the energy dialogues with russia and ukraine. those dialogues have provided us with the contacts necessary to impress our concerns and views upon both parties in a framework of mutual trust and common interest. at the same time, it clearly underlines the need to give greater momentum to dialogue. thirdly, this dispute has underlined the importance of and the need for a clearer, more cohesive and proactive eu-wide energy security policy. while it is true that the commission and parliament have argued for this for many years, the time is now right to make real progress on this. i should like to stress the importance of developing a common approach to energy, which was highlighted at the hampton court informal summit and in the meeting between the presidency and the commission at the start of the austrian presidency. in his speech today, the president-in-office clearly indicated the importance the presidency attaches to this particular issue and that many concrete and clear proposals have been made. during the crisis we witnessed a certain lack of transparency in the european gas market that has made it quite challenging to monitor and assess accurately how this shortfall was being handled. the 2004 directive concerning measures to safeguard the security of gas supplies, once fully transposed, should assist. addressing those kinds of issues is one of the objectives of the energy market observation system which is under development in my services. more generally, this incident has thrown into sharp focus our increasing dependency on external energy supply. the necessity of adopting and developing a common eu approach will be addressed in a green paper on energy policy that the commission is currently preparing. clearly, the development of a common approach to the external energy dimension will be a fundamental element in the green paper. this external energy dimension should be based on a diversification of different energies, as well as on different energy sources, routes, suppliers and transit networks. there is a clear need for more investment in lng terminals, in gas pipelines for diversification of supplies and gas storage facilities. while the eu has been engaged, via its technical assistance programmes, in promoting the development of new supply routes, and upgrading and enhancing existing routes, it is clear that other major energy consumers also take a very proactive and political approach to this issue. europe will have to learn some lessons here, although one should not underestimate the complexity of this task. there are also, of course, the internal aspects of an eu energy policy to consider: firstly, the need to ensure that an internal eu-wide energy market is a practical reality. there is still some way to go to achieve a real internal market in both electricity and gas. then there is the need to facilitate the necessary infrastructure investments required to ensure that the various national energy markets in the eu can really become more integrated. here it is important for us all to recognise that this calls for the necessary means also to be provided including, where necessary, financial support. we also need to ensure that sufficient policy and financial support is given to research in priority areas and to ensure that more efficient energy technologies, including cleaner coal and renewable energy technologies, can penetrate the market. we need more actively to pursue policies and measures that can achieve real energy savings and efficient use of energy and thus diminish our external dependency. we have adopted ambitious legislation. now it is time to implement it. finally, we need to improve energy security measures to enhance the solidarity mechanisms to face the challenges of possible disruptions to energy supplies. one should keep in mind that this particular dispute, as it affected the eu, was resolved in a very short time, but we must be prepared for longer-lasting disputes. in conclusion, this dispute has again been a real wake-up call for us all. while it is true that energy is just a commodity, it is a commodity that is fundamental for our continued economic development and wellbeing. we must learn the lessons from this episode, which i will sum up as a need for a common european energy policy. this policy needs to be clear, coherent and effective both internally and externally, corresponding to the goals of security of supply, competitiveness and sustainability. (applause)
on behalf of the ppe-de group. – mr president, the recent gas supply crisis is a wake-up call for the european union. the ppe-de group welcomes the fact that the security of energy supply and sustainability of energy production and consumption are one of the austrian presidency’s priorities. it is high time, since energy security is becoming increasingly important for the overall security of the european union, and especially its economic security. any difficulty, even temporary, that has the effect of reducing supplies of energy from third states also causes serious disturbances in the economic activity of the union. we were recently made aware of how the problem of energy security does not solely concern the areas of industry or economics. energy has been used as a weapon and foreign policy instrument, and hence should be discussed in the context of foreign and security policy. the recent energy crisis between russia and ukraine has exposed the vulnerability of many member states of the european union that are to a dangerous extent dependent on one supplier. it is absolutely essential, therefore, for the eu to extend joint action to the energy field and take steps to create a proactive energy policy. it is clear that all the efforts taken at national level are not sufficient as they do not guarantee the long-term interests of the union as a whole. action at eu level is therefore clearly justified, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity. moreover, if we treat the idea of a common market seriously, we should endow economic operators, not to mention citizens, with equality in energy security and supply. in this light we assess very positively the presidency’s plans to finalise the decision on the trans-european energy network early this year. we should, however, move beyond that. one of the main principles of european integration – that of solidarity – encompasses the obligation to assist all those states that are in danger or in difficulty, avenues for enhancing the union’s energy self-sufficiency should be explored. nor should we forget the principles of transparency and equal access. the eu should propose a code of conduct on relations with its main energy suppliers. we should make all the necessary efforts to establish new sources of financing for all the undertakings aimed at increasing the eu’s energy security, both from the eib and from the eu budget itself. we should not just think about ourselves. energy security should constitute one of the cornerstones of the neighbourhood policy. reality calls for courage. close cooperation in the energy field and the possibility of sharing energy reserves constitute one of the most effective and indispensable confidence-building measures both within the union and between the union and its neighbourhood. our citizens will appreciate the tangible results of our actions to secure energy supplies. the ppe-de group will be tabling a resolution on this for the next part-session mr. chairman, please! the liberalisation of the sugar market is a complex problem requiring special consideration. this consideration was expressed by the european parliament in its resolution of 10 march 2005 on the future reform of the common organisation of the market in sugar. unfortunately, the european commission ignored it and in july 2005 submitted to us three draft regulations which undermine the spirit of the resolution adopted. the second time parliament was ignored was on 24 november 2005, when the council adopted the final shape of the reform without parliament's opinion and with the opposition of the agriculture ministers of poland and greece. as a result, we have received draft documents which are a violation of european solidarity and seek to reform the sugar market at the expense of smaller countries, especially those newly admitted to the european union, and to concentrate european production in germany and france. the proposed solutions are a win-win for farmers and sugar workers, and a win-win for the big sugar companies. the man and the partnership died in this reform. the new member states have carried out the privatisation of sugar factories. in poland, it was overwhelmingly taken over by foreign capital for a price of only 1/3 of the amount it is now due to receive for shutting down production. the same is true in many other lands. for these reasons and many others, i am calling for all three drafts to be rejected and for a version to be drawn up in accordance with parliament's resolution of 10 march 2005.

mr. chairman, please! we are debating today three reports from the european parliament on sugar market reform. as the representative of the new member state of poland, i would like to raise two serious objections to this reform. first, the need for reform is due to the excessive sugar exports of two countries, namely germany and france, which amount to almost 2 million tonnes, and these countries should bear the costs of the reform by significantly reducing their exports. poland, which exports only 90 000 tonnes, can only reduce its production to this extent. secondly, in poland - unlike in other european countries - sugar production limits are imposed on sugar factories, not on farmers. most of the sugar factories in poland were bought by german and french investors, who paid for them (per tonne of their production limit) around eur 200. with a compensation of eur 730 per tonne of production eliminated, the owners of the sugar mills will receive almost 4 times more than they paid and will still have possession of the post-production assets, i.e. buildings, land, machinery. these two serious reservations are addressed to the commission and the council, the commissioner present, who believe that they have prepared an excellent concept for the reform of the sugar market.
member of the commission. mr president, i have listened carefully to the debate. its intensity is a sign that quite a lot is at stake. however, it is also a sign of the commitment with which you have engaged yourselves in the process of making this new reform. let me first deal with the amendments. i believe that i have found in them a lot of common ground with my own views. i shall start with the proposed new common market organisation. you have argued that the safety net is necessary during the restructuring period ending in 2009-2010 in order to limit undesirable market disturbances. i can accept that. i can therefore endorse the substance of amendments 2, 29 and 54. in order not to encourage overproduction and subsequent building-up of stocks, it will be necessary to set the intervention price at a level considerably lower than the reference price of the following campaign. intervention will also have to be limited to a certain maximum quantity. finally, i think that during the restructuring period we need to dispose of all management tools, including private storage. you also argue that as long as our international commitments are respected some quantities of quota sugar should or could be exported. for the sake of the market balance, this is an idea that i can live with and thus i accept in principle amendments 20, 39, 49, 51 and 68. many of you have mentioned bioethanol. i share your analysis that future energy production could become a major outlet for community beet. along these lines, i can support amendments 11 and 42, raising the political profile of bioethanol in the reform package. as you are aware, the commission is working on a whole set of political initiatives. on 1 february we shall adopt a proposal on the promotion of biofuels contributions have been adopted, rather than to take it now within the context of the sugar reform. i must underline that i am very interested in coming back to this debate as it is very important. i provisional extension of the quota without restructuring levy for the marketing year 2006/2007. the commission can thus agree with the principle of amendments 23 and 69. i can share your concerns as regards the income of beet growers, and consent to the relevant part of amendment 31 concerning the removal of the additional 10% flexibility for the sugar price. on industrial sugar, i can accept the substance of amendment 43. strict and complex rules that are difficult to monitor should be avoided. there is also a series of technical amendments that were already accepted in the technical amendments on the reform of the com. let me now move to the draft regulation amending council regulation (ec) no 1782/2003 establishing common rules for direct support schemes. i can support the principle of increased flexibility for member states in the context of the compensatory payments and therefore accept the substance of amendments 5, 6, 8 and 11, adjusted as necessary. building on my vision to underpin the development of bioethanol production in the community, i can also live with the notion of amendment 7, whereby sugar beet for purposes other than sugar production could be grown on set-aside land. amendment 4 and amendment 13 present a compensation system based on the amount of sugar produced from beet from each individual farmer. i am in favour of the proportionality principle of this reform, for instance, by advancing higher levels of compensation to member states facing severe reductions on their quotas. however, the draft report proposes a system that would differentiate payments based on the volume of the sugar beet produced. such a system would create enormous practical difficulties for a very limited added value, which would go against the shared objective of simplification, and i therefore cannot accept it. nor can i accept the other amendments. finally, let me refer to the draft regulation establishing the restructuring funds. i can endorse the idea underlying amendments 4 and 14, whereby beet growers can benefit from a part of the restructuring aid. however, given the very different conditions faced by member states, a minimum of 50% would be too high. let us not forget the many obligations that need to be dealt with through this restructuring fund. there are some environmental, and some social obligations that are very important. if we were to impose a minimum of 50%, there would be cases where we would have difficulty in meeting these different obligations. therefore i cannot accept it. as mentioned already in my opening statement, a minimum of 10%, with the possibility for the member states to increase this percentage, seems much more appropriate. mrs mcguinness, this is addressed specifically to you: i would never dare interfere in the decisions taken by the member states to decide at what level they would agree on this compensation percentage. likewise, i can support the principle set down in amendment 5, and the relevant part of amendment 10, relating to the extended flexibility for industries ceasing sugar production and moving to alternative sectors, such as the production of bioethanol. the same applies to the notion of the partial quota surrender which is in amendment 7. the social element is already well covered in the proposal and additional administrative requirements would only slow down the restructuring process. therefore, i am of the view that amendments 6, 9 and the relevant part of amendment 7 should not be accepted. some last-minute amendments have also been tabled. i am positive about the idea of amendment 17. sugar beet growers who continue sugar beet production in member states which significantly reduce their sugar quota should be eligible for some kind of state aid for a transitional period. the proposed amendments to which i have not referred are of minor importance and for technical reasons i do not consider it necessary to take them on board. this also includes the last-minute amendments tabled last week. i took note of the particularly harsh comments that were made concerning the treatment of the acp countries. indeed, this has been the subject of very intense discussion, but we have not forgotten the acp countries. the foreseen price cut only kicks in for the acp countries in 2008, two years after it is imposed on the european farmers. let us not forget that after the full implementation of the reform, the acp countries will still benefit from a price that is twice as high as the world market price. the commission has always proposed an action plan for the acp countries, with eur 40 million for 2006. these funds are expected to be at their disposal in 2006, even if the prices are not lowered until 2008. funding of eur 40 million is certainly not a lot, but it is enough to get started and it has always been the intention to provide significant additional funds for the remaining period from 2007 to 2013. it is quite clear that the 2005. i have operated in full transparency throughout the process to allow parliament to play its role to the fullest. but, finally, let me say to those of you who are critical here today that we owe the next item is the recommendation for second reading drawn up by mrs eija-ritta korhola on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the application of the provisions of the aarhus convention on access to information, public participation in decision-making and access to justice in environmental matters to community institutions and bodies (06273/2/2005 - c6-0297/2005 - 2003/0242 (cod)) (a6-0381/2005).
member of the commission. i would like to thank the speakers tonight for their very important speeches. i shall make an assessment of the main amendments, while at the same time responding to the main points raised today. with regard to access to environmental information: the commission cannot accept amendments nos 4, 14 and 15 which seek to apply the system of derogations from the provisions of directive 2003/2004 on access to environmental information and requests for information addressed to the community institutions. the proposed regulation extends to all community institutions the existing horizontal community legislation on access to documents, as provided for in regulation 1049/2001. the european parliament's amendments in question could have the side effect of creating two, partly overlapping, access regimes to documents, which would not contribute to transparency and legal clarity. the new article 6 of the common position already covers these exceptions and access to environmental information which, in any case, must be explicitly specified in the light of the requirements of the aarhus convention. amendments nos 7 and 12, which seek to include the degree of progress of infringement proceedings in the definition of environmental information, cannot be accepted. the aarhus convention does not provide for such a provision. in addition, infringement procedures are not environmental information in themselves. however, it should be noted that it is the commission's practice to publish on its website information concerning its decisions on infringement procedures for all policy areas. the commission can accept amendment no 16, which provides for a period of 15 working days for informing those who have requested access, in the event that the community institution does not have the requested information, and for referring them to the public authority alleged to have the information. as regards public participation, the commission cannot accept its extension to policies, as was sought in amendment no 5 and partly in amendments nos 19 and 20. the aarhus convention encourages public participation in policy preparation under a best effort clause. this is a very broad concept and no such requirement is contained in the legislation addressed to the member states. it should be noted, however, that current practice at community level involves public consultation of stakeholders in the formulation of community policies. in addition, the definition of environment-related projects and programmes is broad and covers programmes of a strategic nature. the commission cannot accept that public participation should also be required for projects and programmes financed by the community institutions, as provided for in amendment no 8. the aarhus convention refers to public participation in projects and programmes when they are prepared by public authorities. in addition, the authorisation of infrastructure projects with significant environmental impact is carried out at member state level with public participation. the commission is able to accept part of amendment no 19 as regards the extension of the deadline for comments in the context of written consultations from four to eight weeks. it can also accept amendment no 20 which adds the obligation for the community institution to take due account of the outcome of public participation. this obligation is derived from the aarhus convention and is in line with the commission's current administrative practice. the commission cannot accept amendment no 23, which would extend the circle of organisations entitled to request internal review from non-governmental organisations whose main objective is to protect the environment to those which also or alternatively promote sustainable development. this criterion would be very difficult to define and would probably cover a wide range of organisations for which it would be unjustified to grant, for environmental purposes, the right of access to such a review procedure. the recognition of a special status for environmental non-governmental organisations, whose main statutory objective is to protect environmental interests, is fully in line with the spirit of the aarhus convention. the commission is also unable to accept the last amendment proposed by the rapporteur, namely that non-governmental organisations should operate in more than one member state, as regards the criteria for the legalization of non-governmental organisations. while it is true that the commission's original proposal referred to action at community level, during the discussions prior to the common position it became clear that such a decision would create unjustified barriers to the right of access to justice. the commission considers this provision in the common position to be satisfactory, which refers to the community dimension of the environmental objective which the non-governmental organisation should promote within the community. finally, amendments nos 22, 24 and 25 concern the outcome of the internal review of administrative acts adopted by the community institutions, in accordance with article 10, and the relationship with the provisions on access to the european court of justice, in accordance with article 12. for the reasons already stated in my original position, the commission cannot accept them because they would be in breach of the provisions of the treaty on the standing of parties. the commission can accept in principle amendments nos 26 and 27 concerning the adjustments to the procedural rules and the date of application of the regulation. i am forwarding to the secretariat of parliament a complete list of the commission's views on the amendments.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on wednesday at 12 noon.

member of the commission. mr president, this has been a very valuable discussion on the human rights clause and on human rights and democracy in general. let us not forget that human rights issues are already being raised systematically with partners in political dialogues. we have established dedicated human rights dialogue and consultations with certain countries, and human rights subcommittees have also been established. in other cases, human rights may be raised at association councils and at association committee meetings. the purpose of the human rights clause is not simply to make it possible to impose sanctions, but also to create a basis for human rights dialogue and for the setting-up of institutions concerned with it, because we need to give such institutions a chance and encourage them to develop. institution building is as important as the clause, and the existence of the human rights clause in the association agreement, or in partnership and cooperation agreements, creates the basis for this. therefore there is no need to replicate this in sectoral agreements. i also want to recall that our agreements have a wide range of policy goals. we want to contribute to stability and to the increase of welfare for all the populations concerned. it is not a lack of courage if we do not always have the same human rights clause or if we do not apply sanctions. we also have to contribute to the development of a population – look at the african, and some asian, populations, as some of you mentioned. there is also freedom from want and freedom from fear, which are closely related to human rights and to the human security concept. that means we cannot throw the baby out with the bathwater. there are many other clauses to defend, such as the clause against terrorism, the clause against weapons of mass destruction and the clause for democracy. it is all interlinked and we cannot focus only on human rights; we have to see the whole picture, which includes poverty eradication. this is the difficult balance that we have to strike sometimes. it is not easy to harmonise this clause, because we are negotiating with every partner and we have to find solutions in the end. not every partner accepts exactly the same wording. however, it is not so much about wording but about application and the way we can encourage the partners to come up with their own solutions, because, as we have always made clear, we do not want to impose everything on the others: we want to encourage their societies to build and to change. as i have already said, institution building is just as important, as are legal, judicial and police reform, because that is where human rights are applied. finally, i should like to say that, with all due respect, in many individual cases we have been able to get people out of prison and to talk about them. we speak about the death penalty with each and every partner, we speak against torture, and slowly these things come through. maybe sometimes the issue is speed – not everything is being done at the same time. but let us be realistic: we cannot change the world in a day.

mr. chairman, please! i welcome the fact that the facilitation of local border traffic has taken the form of a regulation. this means that these regulations will be applied directly by all countries throughout the european union without the need to implement them into national legal systems. this regulation is of particular importance for the union as a whole, but in particular for those states which are responsible for security at the external borders: poland, my country, has the longest external land border in the european union, and we welcome the facilitation that the regulation brings. it is clear that there is a different dimension to the border for the inhabitants of the interior, the central part of each country, and another for the inhabitants of the border regions. for these last ones, the boundaries are part of their daily lives, they are their constant, practical experience. they're the ones who have to live with the consequences of her existence. and that is why i hope that there will be no difficulties and no administrative blockages, because borders cannot be an obstacle to cultural, social and regional cooperation. what does the regulation give us in terms of content? the regulation ensures equality within the union, solidarity with its close neighbours, a sense of unity and the abolition of artificial divisions, and will also stimulate cooperation between regions. in practice, however, i am convinced that it will eliminate the queues at the consulates of those countries which have granted visas, and at the same time eliminate corruption in the issuing of these documents. the last sentence. with this regulation, if we adopt it, we send a signal that the european union is not an inaccessible fortress, it is not a european fortress. the union is not only abolishing internal borders, but is also opening up to the outside world. and a bit pathetically, our nearest neighbours will be able to enter with their heads held high, albeit briefly, and not - as so far - on their knees.
mr. chairman, please! the introduction of facilitation at external borders in local border traffic is a step in the right direction. however, much will depend on the member states themselves implementing the provisions of this regulation. the question is whether the target group of beneficiaries of such a move will be large and whether the reasons for introducing the regime coincide with those indicated in the draft regulation, namely family and social cohesion, cultural or economic cooperation. the ability of neighbouring countries to ensure full reciprocity for the effective implementation of readmission agreements will also be a challenge. when implementing the low-traffic regime, member states will have to take a very responsible approach to prevent the new bis system from being used for cross-border crime, smuggling or organising illegal immigration. it can therefore be concluded that the project under discussion is only paving the way for the establishment of local border traffic at our external borders and that its actual establishment must be continuously monitored through a cost-benefit analysis in terms of the real benefits for the communities living in border areas in accordance with security requirements. the assessment of this may differ in the different member states on the external borders of the union. in conclusion, if we are serious about talking about comprehensive solutions to make our external borders friendly to traveling third-country nationals, while maintaining all the necessary security requirements, we should coordinate the efforts of all institutions and member states to ensure the full and rapid application of the schengen acquis by the ten new member states, which will benefit from the possibility of issuing short-term schengen visas, with a more transparent visa policy towards their neighbours. in addition, the possibility of extending the use of national long-stay multiple-entry visas should be jointly considered where the use of local border traffic in the proposed form is not cost-effective and attractive to the border community, which is more interested in facilitating access to the entire territory of the neighbouring country rather than to a narrowly delineated area.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, i would like again to thank the rapporteur, the shadow rapporteurs and all the speakers. thanks to the contribution of each institution, the balance between facilitation on the one hand and security on the other has been maintained and this regulation, as was rightly said, will also be very helpful in strengthening the local development of important european regions near to the external borders. the introduction of a specific local border traffic permit for border residents will help in identifying those people who have the right to benefit from the facilitated border crossing regime. member states will have the right to scrutinise carefully people requesting this permit. however, i think that is fully justified by the advantages deriving from such a permit. first of all, holders of the permit will no longer need to be in possession of a visa, and a visa exemption for the holders of a local border traffic permit will be included very soon in the forthcoming commission proposal revising the relevant visa regulation which i will put forward by the end of march. later in the spring i will also present the new document on the common consular instruction for issuing a visa. on the basis of this regulation, member states will be able to provide some practical facilitation such as specific border crossing points reserved for border residents and give them the possibility in very exceptional cases to cross the border outside authorised border crossing points. to counterbalance that, member states will have to ensure regular surveillance of border areas in order to avoid the misuse of the local border traffic regime and provide for specific sanctions. finally, the commission will report on the implementation of the local border traffic regime two years after the entry into force of the regulation, proposing modifications if necessary. i would like to conclude my remarks by stressing that i very much hope parliament will confirm with its vote its support for the proposal made by the rapporteur, and i will encourage the council to do the same as soon as possible. mr. chairman, please! the dozens of decisions taken by the european parliament sometimes include decisions that affect the future of the european union. the services directive is of this nature. it is intended to serve the fundamental principle of european freedoms. this is to ensure that there is no discrimination in the provision of services within europe on grounds of nationality, and that citizens of the old and new member states are treated on the same basis. their implementation will serve both economic growth and the spread of the european social model. the practice of economic freedom does not weaken but strengthens the social dimension of europe. the search for compromise is certainly essential in the work of parliament and in this case too, regardless of our differences of opinion, we should do so. however, there are limits to this action, beyond which the services directive may lose all meaning. i think it is wise not to market those areas where the logic of the market does not work. i think it is reasonable to confirm that the directive does not affect labour law. however, i see no reason to introduce exceptions to the directive which are unjustified, which have no clear legal content. and i think that in matters of such strategic importance, the law needs to be clear. we need a sensible, forward-looking decision, the ghosts of the polish plumber or frankenstein should disappear from european thinking in favour of trust, freedom and solidarity. mr. chairman, please! the european union is founded on four freedoms: the free movement of goods, capital, labour and services. these pillars of the european community were written in 1958 because it was already clear that they were a necessary condition for real integration in europe. even after several decades, we still do not have free movement of services in europe. i see the main reason for this as the weakness of the political class. politicians were unable or unwilling to explain to citizens that freedom to provide services meant new jobs and faster economic growth. instead of explaining the meaning of the enlargement of the european union and showing the opportunities created by competition, politicians prefer to frighten voters with social dumping, the "frankenstein" directive and the "polish plumber". in this climate, the european parliament is debating today a services directive whose implementation will make life easier for consumers and businesses, significantly boost economic growth and create 600 000 new jobs in europe. unfortunately, there is a growing attack on the directive from populist and protectionist positions. repeatedly, there are unsubstantiated assessments that opening up the services market will lead to social dumping and deterioration of employment conditions. but there is still a compromise. i would remind you that the directive excludes employment and labour law issues, which goes against the concerns expressed by trade unions. public services have also been shut down. i believe this will strike a balance between the need for competitiveness and the need to protect workers' rights. i therefore call on the european parliament to adopt the directive in a form that will strengthen competitiveness, open up labour markets and make life easier for consumers and businesses.

member of the commission. the sugar quota is in principle fixed per country by community legislation. under the current sugar market organisation, the quotas are allocated by the member states to the sugar manufacturing undertakings and are actually not allocated directly to the beet growers. this principle will remain unchanged after the reform and poland is no exception to this rule. the restructuring fund will be set up in order to facilitate the necessary restructuring measures that should lead to lower sugar production in the less competitive regions within the european union. undertakings which renounce their sugar quota will be eligible for restructuring aid over a transitional period of four years. however, this payment will be linked to a series of conditions, including obligatory consultation with the beet growers and the submission of a restructuring plan to be agreed between the government and the industry. member states will have significant flexibility to lay down detailed rules for the implementation of the restructuring aid, as long as they comply with the general rules of future community legislation. therefore – and this is very important and i underline it at every opportunity – the restructuring money cannot be pocketed by the industry. this is very important and it is the whole idea behind this restructuring fund. besides the undertakings, beet growers and machinery contractors will also be able to benefit from this restructuring fund. an amount of at least 10% of the restructuring fund, amounting to eur 730 per tonne, should be reserved for the farmers, to compensate in particular for investment in the specialised machinery needed to produce sugar beet. it is quite clear, with this wording of ‘at least 10%’, that member states can decide that a higher percentage should be allocated to the sugar beet producers, the farmers. it should also be emphasised that, independently of the restructuring fund that we have just talked about, sugar beet growers will receive direct aid as compensation for their loss of revenue due to the reduction in prices. they will receive this direct aid even if they stop producing sugar beet. this is very important. for the new member states specifically, there will clearly be no phasing-in of the direct payment for the sugar beet compensation. the sugar beet producers in the new member states will receive exactly the same amount per hectare in compensation as the eu-15, which means that there is no phasing-in as there is for cereals. the compensation will be 100% right from when the new sugar reform is first implemented.

who provides comprehensive insurance for the investor-farmer risk associated with the financing of investments, the risk of changes in product prices, the risk of changes in fertiliser, feed, fuel prices, the risk of global climate change, soil degradation, drought, hurricanes, floods and storms? today's debate in defense of human rights, democracy is about defending the armenian cultural heritage that is threatened with total destruction. armenia, a country of four million people, has been the world's first christian country since 301, as evidenced not only by historical records but also by thousands of crosses carved on stone tablets called khachkars, which have been destroyed, as well as other monuments of armenian culture, in azerbaijan, georgia and turkey. chachkaras, or cross-stones, measuring from three to ten feet [0.5 to 3.5 m] high, were made of basalt and placed on a perpendicular base, with the cross facing west. the armenians saw the chakkar as a protective force against natural disasters. they were used to commemorate important events, as compositional elements in sacred buildings, and as tombstones, always at the feet of the deceased. recently, a medieval cemetery in zulfa, a city in the area controlled by azerbaijan, was destroyed. the scandalous process of vandalism and destruction of armenian cultural monuments began in 1998, when as many as 800 such stone crosses were vandalized. although the demolition was halted for a time after unesco protested, it resumed in 2002. most likely, the criminal destruction of armenian national heritage is being carried out with the permission of the azerbaijani authorities, who sent specially trained military units to destroy armenian crossboards. armenians have been persecuted for centuries by wars, aggression, occupation, they are a nation deeply experienced both as a nation and as christians. the azeri on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i'm taking the floor on the merger of two banking groups, unicredito italiano and hvb, which has caused a lot of controversy in poland. in 1999, unicredito acquired a controlling stake in one of the largest polish banks, pekao s.a. it was, as it turned out, a perfect deal. seven years later, their stock is worth four times that. however, by buying the polish bank, the italians undertook not to make a capital investment in any company operating in poland that competed with the bank. the acquisition of shares in hvb, and thus indirectly in another polish bank, bph, is therefore a clear breach of the privatisation agreement, and the polish authorities are even obliged to block the merger and enforce the terms of the agreement. it is worth emphasising that the polish government's aim in this dispute is not to prevent a foreign entity from taking control of a domestic company, as has recently happened in france, spain or italy. therefore, the accusations of protectionism made against the polish authorities are completely unfounded in this case. it should also be borne in mind that while the european commission has powers over mergers with a community dimension, contractual obligations and banking supervision are already national competence. so i hope the european commission will take these arguments into account and end the festival of threats against poland in this matter.
mr. chairman, please! community law regulates mergers and acquisitions in the internal market by establishing a competition policy which is one of the main and earliest agreed community policies. it is intended to ensure that barriers to internal trade within the common market are not replaced by other actions by companies or governments that distort competition. unfortunately, recent events suggest that protectionist and short-sighted measures are being taken in some member states. these include the german e.on bid to take over the spanish endesa, the merger of the french gas giant gaz de france and the international oil and energy group suez based in italy, and more recently the polish government's blocking of the merger of banks pekao s.a. and bph, which is the result of the merger of the german hvb group and the italian unicredito. the objection of the polish government in the light of community law has a dubious legal basis and puts poland in a bad light vis-à-vis foreign investors. unfortunately, this case has also become a tool of the right-wing government's fight against the independence of the national bank of poland, the central bank.

requirements of justice is reached soon. in addition to the case of hissène habré, a pragmatic way forward must be found – as some of you have said – to bring to justice charles taylor, who is currently in exile in nigeria. in terms of funding, we are contributing to the international criminal tribunals of sierra leone and rwanda. in addition, a large project is being prepared for the democratic republic of the congo, which will seek to underpin our work in the icc. finally, states have a duty under international law to try or to extradite those charged with international crimes, such as crimes against humanity, war crimes and genocide. it is primarily, therefore, a matter for the heads of state concerned to ensure that this happens in the cases of hissène habré, charles taylor and mengistu haile mariam. the importance of the role of the international criminal court comes into play when states refuse to observe their duties in this regard. that is why it is so important that the european union should continue to support the universal ratification and implementation of the rome statute.
the greatest enemy of justice is impunity. unnamed crimes, crimes that go unpunished, criminals living with impunity and often in luxury, lead to the trivialization of death and human suffering. the people of africa have suffered greatly at the hands of their rulers. it is our duty to help them. not just material, but also those that are related to higher values, like a sense of justice. modernization has made it possible for bad people to do more harm to others. modernisation should also lead to quicker and more effective prosecution of those who ruthlessly abuse their power. immunities and privileges were designed to protect against the abuse of power, not to protect those who abuse power. great moral authorities can forgive. but there is no true forgiveness without repentance. sadly, criminals who feel neither personal responsibility nor the right of others to judge their actions rarely experience such feelings as repentance. so we have to support actions that will force them to answer the questions: why did they kill, why did they rape, why did they torture? this isn't about revenge. this is about getting back in balance. it's about the balance between right and wrong. without this basic balance, the future of humanity will be in constant danger, and not just in africa.
mr president, mr president of the european commission! unfortunately, 2005 will also be remembered by europeans as the year in which the constitutional treaty was rejected in two of the european union's founding countries. it's a signal to us politicians that we're not listening to our citizens enough. the european union has not yet been united after the last enlargement with ten countries, and the future accession of turkey is already being served. 2007 could be a year of opportunity for a deeper, more united europe if the old member states open up more to the new ones, above all by opening up their labour markets. unfortunately, few countries seem to be more courageous than spain and portugal, which know from recent experience that it is hard to be in the union and at the same time be a second-class european. i propose that future enlargements of the european union be either complete or not at all. i hope that i am also expressing the wishes of the people of the netherlands and france. it is not too late to make europe more integrated by ensuring that its budget is ambitious. the year 2006 brought the energy supply problems to the attention of europeans. europe needs a common energy policy now more than ever. it will also be an opportunity to improve the prospects of farmers, especially in the new member states, by involving them in the production of biofuels. the globalization of the world is an inevitable process. europe should see this as a new challenge, an opportunity for growth. we have a duty to help developing countries, but also to deepen our european social model and to care for the most disadvantaged citizens in our member states.

the next item is the debate on the oral question to the council by mr giles chichester, on behalf of the committee on industry, research and energy (o-0007/2006 - b6-0009/2006).
mr president, energy, as we have recently witnessed, is also sometimes treated as a weapon for exerting political influence by states which enjoy a quasi-monopolistic position, as in the russia/ukraine case. that is what really triggered this sudden interest in energy policy. the problem should therefore be considered as a foreign and security policy issue and so, besides commissioner piebalgs, i would willingly address mr solana and mrs ferrero-waldner. it is essential for the eu to develop a true external security policy dimension in relation to gas and oil deliveries, which is distinct from energy policies sensu stricto. we should not mix them up. the question is, what added value can the eu offer in the event of politically motivated cuts in energy supplies? proposals, as included in the green paper, go in the right direction, although they are still too modest. solidarity, as one of the main principles of european integration, creates an obligation to assist all those member states which are in difficulty. we must extend this solidarity principle to problems related to energy supply shortages caused by political action. what is needed is cooperation and solidarity, not competition among member states in securing external energy supplies, as happens today. the forthcoming spring council should, above all, consider three issues of utmost importance: first, mutual assistance among member states in case of energy supply cuts; second, mutual consultation mechanisms among member states for major gas and delivery contracts; and third, the inclusion of an energy security clause in all eu treaties with third countries, which are either a source of energy or a transit country. an energy security clause should impose an obligation to follow a certain code of conduct and to promise not to use energy delivery as an instrument of political pressure. the time has come to move beyond declarations.
mr. chairman, please! the security of supply in the european union is diminishing with each month of inevitable increase in dependence on imported energy. the only thing we can avoid in this field is unstable and unpredictable partners. their role in the european energy market should be kept within safe limits. to the surprise of many european countries, though not all, russia has recently emerged as this unstable partner. its supply has been limited recently by climatic conditions in siberia, by the lack of security for pipelines in the south of the country, and by the government's unbridled use of energy as a tool of political pressure against its western-oriented neighbors. for this reason, energy cooperation cannot be closed to countries outside the union. it is outside the union that we have energy problems. we also have some of our remedies outside the union, for example in norwegian fields. therefore, not only energy policy but also trans-european networks should extend beyond the borders of the union. the enhanced neighbourhood policy should therefore be enriched by an energy aspect. the polish proposal for an energy pact based on solidarity and boldly going beyond the borders of the union should therefore be discussed more seriously at the forthcoming summit. energy security is primarily a matter of foreign and defence policy. to pretend that the key to providing it is new energy sources or restrictions imposed on industry in the form of, say, climate agreements, is naive. renewable energy will continue to be an expensive addition to our energy supply for a long time to come, and the excessive restrictions on european industry, often backed by questionable scientific evidence, are a factor limiting our competitiveness.
mr. chairman, please! poland is particularly vulnerable to the policy of using natural gas and oil supplies to our country as a tool of political influence by the main supplier of these energy resources, namely russia. hence the polish government's initiative, presented in the forums of the european institutions, to introduce a solution to energy security that can be described as 'one for all, all for one', i.e. the application of the principle of solidarity. unfortunately, it has been met with a rather lukewarm response from the largest european countries, as most of them try to push for solutions that are beneficial to them, even at the expense of other members of the european union. the construction of the northern gas pipeline across the baltic sea, which is the result of an agreement between russia and germany, is a perfect example of such a policy. while this will significantly improve germany's energy security in the future, it is unfortunately detrimental to the economic interests and energy security of countries such as poland, lithuania, latvia, estonia and non-eu countries such as ukraine. the commission is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of renewable energy sources.
mr. chairman, please! after the political speeches, a few technical remarks. energy crises are always caused by the lack of supply of two energy sources to europe: gas and oil. we're not self-sufficient here. we have two choices. firstly, more of europe's own energy sources. second, diversification of supply. more energy ownership means research and applications, higher energy efficiency and renewable energy, as the most important. we forget that europe has huge deposits of hard coal and brown coal. i don't understand why clean coal technologies aren't directly in our parliamentary resolution? others have had research and commercial programs like this for years. nuclear energy is also a necessity, especially with the threat of a greenhouse effect. more money for research and technology should be the obvious demand of the european parliament. secondly, diversification of supply. we have not yet tapped into the enormous potential of one of our neighbors, ukraine. last night, not far from here in solvay, the ukrainian government presented these possibilities - its own gas reserves, the largest natural gas reservoirs in europe, transit of oil and gas from turkmenistan and the caspian sea independently of gazprom. all of this can be the subject of eu-ukraine cooperation. it requires leaving the ukrainian pipelines in ukrainian hands. this requires investment, construction and repair of pipelines, which we, the european union, should be helping ukraine to do. we have the european development bank, the trans-european networks, the enhanced neighbourhood policy. we can become more united and secure, and we have the basis for a common energy policy for the european union.
mr. chairman, please! the union's energy policy has two dimensions: external, geopolitical and internal, as energy security also means the rationalisation of energy use. europe must now manage its energy potential and improve its use by eliminating thermodynamic imperfections: for example, by thermomodernising buildings, but not only; by modernising and expanding the use of distributed heat and power sources, especially in the new countries of the european union, where there is a huge potential for cogeneration and wasted energy; by making prudent use of renewable sources, especially biomass, the use of which for electricity generation, however, i consider to be somewhat ambiguous. the enlarged european union, by creating cross-border networks, can exploit the fact that there are significant time shifts from its eastern to its western borders, leading to a reduction in peak loads on the electricity grid and, in the north-south direction, to a better use of seasonal temperature differences. the energy-intensive nature of national income needs to be further reduced, and this must also be reflected in customs policy. therefore, it is not understandable to maintain a 6% duty on highly energy-intensive primary aluminium. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the union's energy supply is not affected by the price pressure.

the next item is the debate on the report drawn up by mr csaba őrye on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs on transitional rules restricting the free movement of workers within the eu labour markets [2006/2036 (ini) ] (a6-0069/2006).
member of the commission. ladies and gentlemen, thank you, but i'm used to the fact that when i give a report, the reporter speaks first and the commissioner responds afterwards. but if you've decided to change that, i'm ready to step down. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank mr őrry for his excellent report on a subject which is one of the pillars of european integration. the transitional measures provided for in the treaty of accession aim to enable the member states to prepare progressively for the achievement, as rapidly as possible, of the single and irrevocable objective of granting to all migrant workers who are nationals of countries which joined the european union in 2004 free access to employment in all member states, which is one of the fundamental freedoms enshrined in the treaty of rome. as provided for in the treaty of accession, the commission has assessed the functioning of these transitional measures for the first two-year phase in order to help member states to take decisions as to whether to maintain or abolish the transitional measures. on the basis of statistical data covering 2004 and sometimes the period 2005 and after consulting the various stakeholders, the commission has reached certain conclusions regarding the first stage of the transition period. the number of registered workers since accession is generally very low, rarely reaching 1% of the host country's active population. moreover, the arrival of workers from the new member states seems to have had a generally positive effect. enlargement has helped to bring the black economy of eu-8 workers out of the shadows. accession has also contributed to reducing labour shortages and improving economic performance in europe. countries that did not introduce restrictions after may 2004 have experienced stronger economic growth, reduced unemployment and increased employment. the workers who have been able to gain legal access to the labour market here have been able to integrate easily. it is clear that only member states decide whether or not to apply transitional measures, but the commission may nevertheless invite member states to objectively assess the advantages and disadvantages of transitional measures. in fact, this second stage is a genuine transitional stage which is supposed to bring us closer, either wholly or at least partially, to the goal of free movement of labour. in this spirit, member states applying restrictions under the act of accession cannot treat eu-8 nationals already legally resident on their territory in a more restrictive way than third-country nationals who are long-term residents, as announced at the previous plenary session. an explanatory letter on this subject was sent to the home affairs ministers to clarify the legal situation. in the previous minutes the rapporteur mentioned this problem of third-country nationals, so let me stress once again that in the context of the directives and the accession treaties it is not possible to grant to third-country nationals who are long-term residents in the territory of the member states of the european union more favourable treatment than that accorded to citizens who are nationals of a european union state, i.e. if certain restrictions apply to european union citizens, they logically apply to third-country nationals who are long-term residents in the territory of the european union. for the same reasons, the commission also monitors compliance with the provision that member states may not restrict access to their labour market for eu-8 workers more than before the date of signature of the accession treaty, i.e. before 16 april 2003. the commission also supports the call on member states to strictly apply community legislation, in particular in the field of posting of workers. i recognize that we must definitely strengthen the statistical monitoring of the flow of workers within the european union, on behalf of the alde group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the report by mr őra on the transitional system restricting the free movement of workers in the labour markets of the european union must be assessed on the basis of four, in my view, fundamental criteria. first, the free movement of persons is one of the four fundamental freedoms of the single market and is a right of all citizens of the european union. the abolition of transitional periods as soon as possible is therefore a requirement for the recognition of that right. this does not mean that mass mobility within the european union should be promoted. mobility due to the need to seek work must be distinguished from the freedom of movement of persons, which is a civil right. secondly, the report rightly states, and here confirms the european commission's view, that the opening up of labour markets has been beneficial for those countries which have given up transition periods. however, the benefits and risks of free movement of persons for the countries of origin of the citizens who move should also be considered. thirdly, it is important that nationals of member states are not discriminated against against by third-country nationals in the labour markets of the european union. this does not mean, of course, that we are indifferent to the interests of third country nationals and do not wish to express our solidarity with them. finally, the free movement of persons should be seen as an important element of the european social model. as the report by mr őra and the position of the committee on employment and social affairs take account of the above criteria, the alde group will vote in favour of the report, thanking mr őra for the work done.
mr. chairman, please! the latest oecd report indicated that the most developed countries in the union are sweden, finland and the united kingdom. two of these countries opened up their labour markets, but ireland also saw gdp growth as a result of this decision. the report debunks the myth that the influx of workers from outside the country has a destructive effect on the country's economy. it's the opposite. in this employment policy we should be looking for a way out of the lisbon strategy. open labour markets in all the countries of the union. concerns about an influx of cheap labor have not been confirmed. there is limited labour migration. i therefore believe that it is necessary to remove all barriers which could in any way impede the free movement of workers in europe.
