madam president! the european commission reviews the implementation of community law every year. we are now discussing the 21st and 22nd annual reports of the commission. to give an idea of the scale of the problem, it is worth mentioning that the case concerns almost 4 000 infringement proceedings, of which almost 1 000 have been the subject of a reasoned opinion and over 400 have been referred to the court of justice. it is regrettable that the commission only submitted its 22nd annual report in january 2006 with a delay, and therefore parliament can only refer in its resolution to part of the commission's information for 2004. paradoxically, the more complaints, the better. this is because they show that the citizens of the member states play an important role in the process of control and hence in the establishment of eu law. these citizens' actions are not symbolic, they build a citizens' europe and, in general, they effectively control the application of eu law. committees of the european parliament should pay close attention to the application of community law, especially in situations where the member responsible for drawing up the report is required to take an active part in monitoring the implementation of the legislation in question in the individual member states of the european union, which should then result in a call for immediate correction of such shortcomings if they are identified. to improve the smoothness of this process, the internal procedure should be shortened, as was rightly done in the european parliament's draft resolution, and the individual commissioners should be given powers to directly supervise the transposition of community legislation into national law within the required time limits. we shall achieve this by empowering the commissioners to address calls directly to the member states to correct irregularities, of course in the field of activity of each of them.

madam president! better law-making in the european union requires well-formulated and transparent legislation and its prompt and correct implementation and application. there are still too many cases of incorrect implementation of community law, which are the result both of poor quality legislation and of deliberate action by member states to undermine community legislation for political, economic or administrative reasons. moreover, in many member states, national courts are still reluctant to apply the principle of the primacy of community law. if eu law is not seen as binding on everyone and its transposition and implementation depends only on the good will of the government, this may lead, as mrs frassoni rightly points out in her report, to an objective renationalisation of community policies, which will of course have a negative impact on the internal market and the entire legal acquis of the union. inconsistencies in transposition can also lead to the misapplication of union law by introducing different provisions in different countries, thus undermining the credibility of the community. if we cannot demand that the governments of the member states correctly transpose eu law, we cannot expect citizens to trust that the eu institutions, such as the commission, the council or the european parliament, will effectively protect their rights under eu law.

and now the european council - have decided in principle to take appropriate action against those responsible for human rights violations and violations of democratic rules in belarus. the council is now preparing a decision to specify and implement this. a whole series of people will be banned from entering the country, including the president himself. the european council also made this clear in its statement accompanying the conclusions. the european union attaches great importance to respect for human rights and the building of democracy throughout the world. it must pay even more attention to what is happening just beyond its borders. the last dictatorship in europe has painfully re-opened its sinister face. the falsification of elections, the persecution of political opponents, the suppression of freedom of speech and assembly are actions of the belarusian regime. we support the belarusian opposition because they are fighting for something that is standard in our country, for freedom and democracy. the belarusian opposition is also fighting for the sovereignty of the country, which is threatened by the dictator's sick and anti-national ambitions. we support the opposition not because of political sympathies, but because of the goals for which it has undertaken to fight. on the other hand, we should do everything possible to make life difficult for the lukashenka regime. if someone doesn't respect the values that we hold dear, they shouldn't be able to benefit from them. the dictator's henchmen should know that europe is not for them. europe is for those who respect freedom, democracy, the rule of law. aleksader milinkiewicz says that dictatorship will not last long, that it can be felt in the air. i wish the people of belarus and all of europe that these words will prove prophetic. may the optimism of those who fight for freedom... give them wings to fly... and lead to the overthrow of the tyrant.
the president of the council. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. what a difference! a few minutes ago the democratic spectrum compared with belarus. they were - apart from some technical flaws and inadequacies - free and fair and gave the ukrainian voters the opportunity to make their choice unhindered and well informed after an active and open fair election campaign under the observation of a free press. the international observers have also noted this. this is a great success for all of us, a success for europe, for the european union, for the osce and for the council of europe. we are pleased to note that these elections were held under the conditions we would like to see. the elections also showed that the ukrainian people have taken ownership of democracy in their own country. this is a milestone in the process of consolidating a democracy that began with the so-called orange revolution. what is particularly important to me and therefore also fitting that the two debates on belarus and ukraine are taking place at the same time : the elections set a new and welcome already come a long way - and in the economic, social and political fields. we, the european union, want to help.

mr. chairman, please! in the debate on the implementation of the 2004 budget, i would like to draw your attention to a number of issues which i consider important in relation to the control of the implementation of the budget. we have received a very comprehensive report from the european court of auditors. a dozen reports on the implementation of the 2004 budget were also presented in this room. but despite all this material, we still know very little about how the budget was actually implemented and how the funds were spent. this is because, first, the information contained in the court's report is rather general in nature, since the court examines mainly the conformity of accounting records, the so-called 'accounting reality', which, as life shows, often deviates from objective reality. secondly, the court's findings after the audit often fail to answer the most important questions as regards the assessment of the rationality of the implementation of the budget , such as: what is the purpose of the funds, whether the funds actually achieve the objectives pursued, whether there is no abuse in their expenditure and, finally, whether there is no waste of funds. the answers to these questions are essential for the presentation of a factual assessment of the implementation of the budget. the need for such knowledge is demonstrated by the findings of direct audits carried out by the auditors of the european court of auditors on the implementation of the tacis programme. nearly seven billion euro was spent on this programme between 1991 and 2005. the programme was designed to provide financial support to the european union's partner countries in eastern europe and central asia, which are currently in a transition phase. for example, in 2005 these were belarus, georgia, kazakhstan, kyrgyzstan, moldova, russia, tajikistan, turkmenistan, ukraine and uzbekistan. the programme was to achieve 29 specific objectives. the court's auditors found that only five had been implemented. if we were to examine most of the programmes financed by the european union budget in the same way, we would be able to determine how rationally and efficiently the eu funds are being spent. however, even this general audit has allowed the european court of auditors to conclude, for the eleventh time in succession, as i would like to emphasise, that the financial statements presented are not free from defects. it therefore seems that the european union needs a comprehensive expenditure control system with a strong involvement of the national control bodies of the member states. only reports prepared under such a system would allow the questions raised above to be answered and the conclusions drawn from such audits could contribute to improving the efficiency of budgetary expenditure in the years to come.

mr. chairman, please! i believe that mr maat's report is reaching the european parliament at a time when there is a genuine expectation that the problem of eels in europe will be solved. the world's cod cod cod catch is estimated at around 200 tonnes. in recent years, however, the catch of this fish has been declining. in 2004, it was only 130 tonnes, and a year later it was only 75 tonnes. the decline in catches has led to a rapid rise in the price of cod, from eur 300 to eur 400 in the mid-1990s to eur 1200 in 2005. as a result, eels were simply unprofitable in europe. the countries with the least access to free cod resources are particularly vulnerable, including most of the baltic states. this is known to be due to the limited migration of the eel from marine to inland waters. the lack of fish in these countries forces them to import fishing gear. however, they face an increasing financial barrier, caused by the rising price of fish in europe. the new baltic states in the european union are being forced to pay huge export prices for this fish to asian countries. in this context, there is a strong call for a system to ensure that the costs of protecting eel stocks are fairly shared by all stakeholders - including, of course, eel exporters and importers.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - i have to go. the state of public finances has a significant impact on economic growth, employment, macroeconomic stability and is an important determinant of the health of the single european currency. the treaty on european union therefore clearly states that developments in the public finance situation in the member states are of interest to the union institutions, including the european parliament. in the exercise of its treaty powers, the european parliament shall once again assess the situation of public finances in the european union and adopt a report thereon. the main message of this year's report is that public finances in most member states are still in an unbalanced state and that this situation has not improved substantially since last year. this requires continued efforts to restore fiscal consolidation. the aggregate deficit of the 25 member states in the european union rose to 2.7% of gdp in 2005 and in the euro area to 2.9% of gdp. as a result, the public debt-to-gdp ratio has been rising steadily for several years and exceeded 70% in the euro area at the end of 2005. since 2003, 11 member states of the european union have had deficits above 3% of gdp and 10 have been subject to the excessive deficit procedure. and what is particularly worrying is that the four largest economies in the european union are among the countries that are not budgetary disciplined: germany, france, the united kingdom and italy. this situation clearly shows that some member states are having serious difficulties in rebalancing public finances, and lack the political will and determination to make the necessary changes. this situation also shows that the preventive and corrective procedures of the stability and growth pact have been ineffective so far. one of the main reasons for this unfavourable budgetary situation is the persistently low rate of economic growth in europe. the lack of necessary structural reforms, growing international competition, and uncertainty about employment prospects and future demand have for many years caused europe to develop more slowly than other regions of the world. policies have not been able to change this situation. expansionary fiscal policies and restrictive monetary policies created an inadequate policy mix and hampered economic growth. the situation is aggravated by the lack of adequate fiscal policy coordination within the euro area. such coordination is essential to enhance the effectiveness of economic policies and to maintain confidence in the single currency, which requires synchronisation in the conduct of fiscal reforms and the avoidance of fiscal imbalances. the underlying stagnation trends in europe are the lack of progress in structural reforms in many member states, including in particular the lack of action to make labour markets more flexible, increase labour force participation, remove barriers in the services market, promote innovation and support entrepreneurship. in this context, the slow progress in implementing the lisbon strategy is of particular concern. madam president! in the report we propose a number of actions to improve the public finances. first, strict and rigorous compliance with the fiscal rules laid down in the revised stability and growth pact is necessary. this will help restore the credibility of the pact and strengthen its disciplinary role. we call for structural action to be accelerated, including in particular the firm implementation of the lisbon strategy. we also propose to take measures to streamline fiscal procedures, increase coordination and improve the effectiveness of fiscal policies. we ask the european commission to analyse the impact that increased fiscal policy coordination could have on economic growth in the union. we recommend improving the quality of fiscal statistics, introducing transparent rules for the valuation of assets and future pension liabilities, taking account of the business cycle in the deficit assessment and extending the budgetary planning horizon to two years. we propose that the principle be adopted that the budgetary structure in the member states is based on a uniform set of macroeconomic assumptions, which could be derived from the european commission. finally, we recommend action to strengthen the incentives for fiscal reform by member states, including through public reporting on the risks of fiscal imbalances. these actions are necessary if fiscal and budgetary policies are to contribute to accelerating economic growth and employment in the european union. the european parliament should send a clear and explicit political signal on this issue. i therefore ask the members to support the report.
madam president! public finance is crucial for economic growth, job creation and macroeconomic stability. the maastricht treaty made it clear that the development of public finances in the member states of the european union should be closely monitored at european union level. the main and important point of this year's report is the unstable budgetary situation of most member states. the countries subject to the excessive deficit procedure included the four largest economies of the european union: france, germany, italy and the united kingdom. the root causes of the difficulties are the continuing slow growth rate in europe and the lack of structural reforms to strengthen public finances for the future. the pace of economic growth in the european union is much slower than its potential would suggest, and much slower than that of other world economic powers such as the united states, japan, china and india. the reason for this is also the low level of domestic demand, the uncertainty about the maintenance of jobs, social security, salaries, pensions. high energy prices, instability in fuel markets and persistent current account surpluses in most asian countries have undermined the confidence of many companies in europe. loose fiscal policies have proved ineffective and have not put our economies on the path to growth. rising debt ratios are a major problem, especially for long-term fiscal stability, across the union. the implementation of the lisbon strategy, launched in 2000, was intended to provide a comprehensive reform agenda. in view of all these problems, i believe that decisive steps should be taken to increase the effectiveness of preventive and corrective measures to strengthen and consolidate public finances.
madam president! in taking part in the debate on the report by mr rosati on public finances, i would like to draw your attention to the following points. first, the recovery of public finances cannot be an end in itself but a means to promote high growth and job creation. secondly, the measures taken by the member states of the european union in this area are unfortunately not producing satisfactory results, as reflected in the falling gdp growth rate from 2.4% in 2004 to 1.5% of gdp in 2005, and in the euro area this fall is even more pronounced: from 2.1% to 1.3% with a persistently high unemployment rate of around 9%. these indicators confirm that the european union is not only not catching up with the united states and other developed countries of the world, but is clearly losing it. it should be added that gdp growth in the united states in 2005 was 3.5%, more than twice that of the european union. third, low economic growth and persistent high unemployment are hampering the substantial reduction of the budget deficit and public debt. in the european union of 25 countries, the budget deficit fell from 3% of gdp in 2003 to 2,6% of gdp in 2004, and in the euro area from 3% to 2,7%, but public debt even increased: from 61,4% in 2002 to 64,1% in 2005, and in the euro area from 69,2% to 71,7%. fourthly, the above data show that the level of budget deficits, and in particular public debt, is clearly higher in the old than in the new member states, and unfortunately the european commission's warnings and recommendations are mainly directed at the latter. finally, fifth, the new member states are undertaking very difficult reforms, including major changes to pension systems. despite the transition from a budgetary system to a capital system - member of the commission. mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen of the house, i would say that it is natural that parliament should demand more from the other institutions and, naturally, i listened very carefully to the speeches. i believe that criticism is necessary if we are to make progress. but i have also noted in mr howitt's report, as in this debate, some positive aspects of our policy, for which i thank you again. in a field such as the promotion and protection of human rights, the balance sheet is naturally mixed. i'd like to share with you my analysis of the situation. firstly, is the union a major player in this area, a player that counts and is counted on? my answer is yes, without a doubt. we all have evidence of that constantly. our partners, whether state or non-state, states or international organisations, continue to look to us and see us as a major player, sometimes even indispensable, because of our political credibility, influence, expertise and the instruments we have. secondly, does the union have the right tools to carry out its action? my answer is yes. we have international instruments at our disposal in the framework of the united nations and the council of europe, to name but a few. we have the framework of our bilateral agreements, which have been widely cited, with the human rights clauses, as well as common political guidelines in many sectors, political dialogues, all kinds of approaches. we have the financial, geographical and thematic instruments, too. thirdly, are our contributions and actions sufficient? i would say no, particularly if the question of our action is posed in global terms. but if we look at specific situations, such as the adoption of the resolution establishing the new human rights council or situations relating to very specific cases of countries and individuals, there are many cases where we have made a difference. in any case, the union, including the member states, is certainly the most important actor with its contributions and actions at the global level, an actor that is really very present, even if we are not always as visible as we would like or as you would like. finally, are we effective in our human rights policy? are we having an impact? i would like, as does parliament, to see us become more effective and more effective. to do this we should make a qualitative leap, especially in terms of consistency. the european union's policy is consistent with that of the individual member states, and the union's political will is consistent with national interests, which are actually manifested at key moments in certain bilateral relations. and we need to better reconcile, in some cases, our multilateral agenda with the bilateral agenda. we also need to mobilise all the institutions of the union, including, of course, the european parliament. as i have said before, we are absolutely in favour of a report drawn up jointly by the three institutions. let us work toward that! parliament can indeed count on me. i'm not sparing myself or my staff. you can count on us for the evaluation, but also for the implementation of human rights policy, even if we too are often faced with a political reality that is not easy to manage. but if we want to improve the impact of our policy, in particular by making our actions more coherent between the european and national levels and between the various institutions, then i think that parliament's annual report, like mr howitt's, must inspire our actions.

member of the commission. mr president, i greatly appreciate that parliament has decided to discuss together the package of instruments for the delivery of external assistance for the future period spanning 2007 to 2013. it is over a year and a half since the commission tabled its proposals. i wish to acknowledge the efforts that have been made by parliament and successive council presidencies to find imaginative and constructive solutions to the challenges that we have encountered on these innovative proposals. the new simplified architecture was the first attempt to streamline all the instruments for external spending. the simplification proposed was welcomed by both parliament and the council. and soon after parliament began its work, a certain number of important questions were raised. these matters were set out in a letter in april last year from the chairman of the foreign affairs committee, mr brok, and the rapporteur for the development cooperation and economic cooperation instrument, mr mitchell. there were six issues in total and on these i believe parliament has obtained full satisfaction. your first concern was to ensure that the instruments were adopted under codecision whenever the treaty made that possible. in response, the council and the commission agreed that the stability instrument should pass from consultation of parliament to codecision. three of the four instruments are codecided. this gives parliament a fully legitimate but unprecedented degree of legislative power over the framework covering external spending. parliament also wished to ensure that the instruments would be subject to a mid-term review and to expiry dates. these points were accepted. we have also agreed that before undertaking the review, parliament should examine the operation of this instrument to identify any dysfunctional situations that may have arisen, and parliament’s report would be considered by the commission in carrying out the review of the instrument. should the review identify problems that require an adaptation of the relevant instruments and regulations, the commission will submit the necessary legislative proposals. that review should be carried out in 2009, as requested by parliament. parliament also wanted separate financial envelopes for different geographic regions and thematic sectors. the commission has provided a breakdown of the envelopes for the codecided instruments and agrees to the inclusion of a breakdown in the regulations. one of the most challenging points has been the involvement of parliament in priority-setting and strategy documents. so far as priority-setting is concerned, the necessary policy elements will be included in the draft regulations. this has been done both for the stability instrument and for the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument. unfortunately, the progress achieved on these instruments has not yet been mirrored in the development cooperation and economic cooperation instrument. parliament’s future involvement in strategy documents is now covered by two declarations annexed to the interinstitutional agreement. i have written to mr brok on how these could be put into practice. we envisage a mechanism for a dialogue with parliament, which should allow us then to present the selected strategy documents, explain our choices and receive parliament’s view on the choices and how the strategy should be implemented. finally, for the development cooperation and economic cooperation instrument, parliament wished to have a clear distinction between policy towards developing countries and towards industrialised countries. we have no difficulty in accepting that. there has been a strong demand from parliament for a separate instrument to support democracy and human rights. in january 2006, the commission set out its vision for the thematic programme on democracy and human rights. i recognise that parliament is not convinced on this. i have listened to parliament and i understand its reasons. i am committed, therefore, to resolving this point to the satisfaction of parliament as part of an overall agreement on the instruments. this is a clear commitment on behalf of the commission to a separate human rights instrument. this position is shared by the council. i should now like to say a few words on each of the instruments that are before this house today. the instrument for pre-accession assistance – the ipa – has been welcomed by parliament for its policy-driven approach. there has been a fruitful dialogue on the proposed regulation with parliament’s rapporteur, mr szent-iványi. indeed, a compromise text for ipa, addressing a number of issues of concern to parliament, was agreed by coreper on 3 may. the commission fully supports this compromise, which reflects to a large extent the amendments proposed by mr szent-iványi in his report. i am pleased to make a formal declaration today, which i hope will also solve the major outstanding issue of parliament’s involvement in the suspension of assistance: ‘the commission will take due account of any request made by the european parliament to the commission to submit a proposal to suspend or restore community assistance, and will provide a prompt and sufficiently detailed reply thereto’. for the stability instrument, i should like to thank the rapporteur, mrs beer, for the central and positive role she has played in the negotiations to date, which have touched on sensitive institutional issues. the report from the committee on foreign affairs has had a very positive impact on the political compromise reached in coreper, for which i thank you. that compromise is very finely balanced. i believe it will form the basis of a deal between the institutions. reflecting concerns of parliament, we have also agreed more policy content under the stability instrument. there are strengthened references to respect for human rights in relation to the fight against terrorism. the commission is ready to make a political declaration further underlining this and confirming its commitment to informing parliament of exceptional assistance measures as they are adopted. i shall be writing to you shortly setting out some ideas on the establishment of a peace-building partnership to improve practical implementation of civilian peace-building projects. for the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument, we have worked intensively with mr szymánski, parliament’s rapporteur, and the presidency. as a result, we now have a text which addresses the concerns of parliament. an agreement on this text was reached in coreper last week and we are very hopeful that, on this basis, an agreement is now within reach. for the development cooperation and economic cooperation instrument, work is not as advanced as for the other instruments. i am convinced that the main building blocks of a compromise are, however, within reach. thanks to the cogent arguments of the rapporteur, mr mitchell, it is agreed that the new legislative set-up must preserve parliament’s codecision rights. it is now a question of the best way to do it. the commission is calling for pragmatism, given our shared objective of achieving genuine simplification of external assistance. in more concrete terms, let me come to the main amendments proposed in mr mitchell’s report. given their total number, i will concentrate on those that relate to the architecture of the instrument. first of all, a series of amendments – amendments 48, 50, 51, 54, 55, 56, 65, 66 and 67 – propose to establish separate policy-setting regulations and a multiannual financial framework to be adopted by codecision in addition to the dceci. this alternative to the incorporation of policy content and financial provisions into the regulation goes against the objective of simplification. the commission is more than willing to expand the geographic and thematic policy content of the dceci to preserve parliament’s rights. we have said so on several occasions. however, we consider that the best way to achieve this is to follow the council presidency’s proposal and to do it in a single regulation. secondly, three amendments – amendments 4, 23 and 114 – reflect one of the general points made by parliament which i referred to earlier: the continuation of an instrument in favour of human rights and democracy. thirdly, five amendments – amendments 1, 5, 6, 23 and 115 – build on the initial request to establish a clear distinction between cooperation with industrialised countries and cooperation with developing countries. they actually go further and propose the splitting of cooperation with industrialised countries from the dceci. the commission understands the underlying concern behind these amendments. the commission could consider, for instance – if this is a condition for a final compromise on a clear and logical structure – the splitting of cooperation with industrialised countries into a separate instrument. fourthly, three amendments – amendments 2, 25 and 26 – call for a change in the legal basis, that is, a single legal basis, article 179, without article 181a of the treaty. i know legal advice differs on this. for the commission, the issue is one of legal security. the commission also understands parliament’s argument that a wide understanding of development cooperation should offer the necessary comfort. i would be ready to re-consider our position if a wide definition of development cooperation based on article 179 is ensured. fifth, one amendment – amendment 51 on sectoral spending targets – is of particular concern. this is the establishment of sectoral spending targets. this would run contrary to the principles of partnership and ownership with beneficiary countries and it would introduce rigidity in programme implementation. there are also a number of other amendments that would need to be discussed in more depth. a document has been submitted to parliament setting out the commission’s position on each of the amendments commission’s position on amendments by parliament in the mitchell report: see annex.. i do not want to give the impression that our positions are far apart on all these issues. out of 117 amendments, the commission can accept 26 in full and 40 in part or in principle. this means that half of the amendments are totally uncontroversial. finally, i should like to say a few words on nuclear safety. this has been an important part of our past work and will remain so. originally included within the stability instrument, the change in the legal basis made it necessary to create a separate instrument for nuclear safety cooperation. i understand that the draft text has now been sent by the council to parliament to allow you to begin preparing your opinion. i should like to finish by saying a few words on the way forward. there are grounds for optimism that agreement could be found on the text of two of the codecided instruments: the stability instrument and the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument. similarly, i hope that the declaration i made concerning the pre-accession instrument is sufficient to allow parliament to give its opinion. what now of the development cooperation and economic cooperation instrument? this is a key element in the architecture. this instrument covers assistance to asia, latin america and south africa, as well as key thematic programmes. it is central to the package and too important to be left behind. i am convinced that we can do what needs to be done to ensure that the complete legislative framework is in place before the end of the year. the presidency has already done considerable work on the policy content of the dceci. there will be a window of opportunity following parliament’s first reading to reach a consensus on the key issues of substance before the adoption of the council’s common position. this could cover some limited changes in the architecture, which would not undermine the principle of simplification and the essential policy provisions. the consensus reached would be reflected in the council’s common position, which the council presidency hopes to adopt in june. this would greatly facilitate a timely agreement on second reading. finally, the provision of effective assistance to our partners from 1 june 2007 onwards is a shared responsibility. with the agreement on the financial perspective and the advances made on this legislative package, i am convinced we are within striking distance of achieving that goal.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. if someone in parliament wanted to use the good cop/bad cop approach to the commission and the council, it would be hard to der rat hält den vertrag zur gründung der energiegemeinschaft zwischen der europäischen gemeinschaft und den ländern südosteuropas in der tat für ein wichtiges instrument, und zwar aus gründen, die evident sind: sicherheit der strom- und erdgasversorgung für die europäische gemeinschaft und auch für die vertragsparteien in der region. dieses thema ist dem österreichischen vorsitz mit einiger dramatik schon nach wenigen stunden im jänner bewusst geworden, als am 1. jänner um 8 uhr morgens die gasversorgung nicht nur der ukraine und moldaus, sondern auch in mitteleuropa gesperrt wurde. damals wurde uns die dramatik der situation allen sehr bewusst. wie der ausschuss sehr zutreffend feststellt, besteht eines der ziele dieses vertrags darin, den energiemarkt der europäischen gemeinschaft auf die länder der region auszudehnen, indem diese den gemeinschaftlichen besitzstand in den bereichen energie, umweltschutz, wettbewerb und erneuerbare energien übernehmen. dies erscheint mir im sinne der homogenität und der kohärenz einer gesamteuropäischen strategie von besonderer bedeutung. der charakter des energiegemeinschaftsvertrags zeichnet sich daher durch die tatsache aus, dass die umsetzung der einschlägigen vorschriften des gemeinschaftsrechts einen der wichtigsten aspekte der arbeit der gremien, die in dem vertrag vorgesehen sind, darstellt. gemäß artikel 25 dieses vertrags ist ferner vorgesehen, dass in übereinstimmung mit der entwicklung des rechts der europäischen gemeinschaft maßnahmen zur änderung des gemeinschaftlichen besitzstandes getroffen werden können. diese dynamische verweisung erscheint mir ebenfalls von großer bedeutung. der rat möchte unterstreichen, dass dies natürlich bedeutet, dass das europäische parlament von beginn an direkt beteiligt ist, wenn gemeinschaftsvorschriften ausgearbeitet und im mitentscheidungsverfahren von unseren beiden institutionen angenommen werden. es sind also vorschriften, die sodann in den rahmen des energiegemeinschaftsvertrages zu übernehmen sind. die bedeutung der rolle des europäischen parlaments bei der annahme des vertrags zur gründung der energiegemeinschaft spiegelt sich auch in der wahl der rechtsgrundlage wider, d.h. in der tatsache, das das europäische parlament über ein zustimmungsrecht verfügt, wie es in artikel 300 absatz 3 des vertrags zur gründung der europäischen gemeinschaft zum ausdruck kommt. es handelt sich also nicht nur um ein recht auf konsultation. die änderung, die der rat an dem von der kommission vorgeschlagenen beschluss über den abschluss des energiegemeinschaftsvertrages vorgenommen hat und auf die der abgeordnete chichester in seiner anfrage bezug nimmt, betrifft die rolle des europäischen parlaments bei der beschlussfassung. in der tat hat der rat absatz 3 von artikel 5 des vorschlags gestrichen, in dem das verfahren der konsultation vorgesehen war. es ist allerdings darauf hinzuweisen, dass die anhörung des europäischen parlaments nach dem kommissionsvorschlag nur in einem einzigen spezifischen fall vorgesehen war, nämlich im falle der festlegung von standpunkten der europäischen gemeinschaften zu beschlüssen, die von der energiegemeinschaft gemäß artikel 100 ziffer (iii) des energiegemeinschaftsvertrags zu fassen sind, das heißt beschlüsse über die ausdehnung dieses vertrags auf weitere energieerzeugnisse und energieträger oder andere wesentliche netzinfrastrukturen. mit anderen worten: gemäß dem kommissionsvorschlag würde die kommission dem rat einen entwurf für die festlegung eines standpunkts der gemeinschaft zu einer solchen änderung des energiegemeinschaftsvertrags unterbreiten, und der rat hätte sodann das europäische parlament zu diesem standpunkt zu hören. hierbei würde es sich jedoch um ein nicht im eg-vertrag vorgesehenes verfahren handeln, dass daher zu den verfahren des vertrags hinzukäme und somit das im vertrag vorgesehene institutionelle gleichgewicht veränderte. im eg-vertrag, nämlich in artikel 300 absatz 2 unterabsatz 3 ist stattdessen vorgesehen, dass das europäische parlament unverzüglich und umfassend zu unterrichten ist. aber auch wenn im eg-vertrag eine ex-ante-unterrichtung des parlaments nicht vorgesehen ist, wenn etwa der vorhin beschriebene fall eintreten sollte, z.b. die ausdehnung des energiegemeinschaftsvertrages – das betrifft die streichung –, so wird der vorsitz des parlaments regelmäßig über alle wichtigen aspekte des beabsichtigten standpunkts des rates unterrichten. ich bemerke in diesem zusammenhang, dass die mitglieder des ausschusses für industrie, forschung und energie sich daran erinnern werden, dass die letzten ratsvorsitze, die mit dieser frage befasst waren, das parlament im rahmen ihrer ausführungen vor diesem ausschuss über den sachstand in bezug auf den energiegemeinschaftsvertrag unterrichtet haben. ich möchte sie ferner darauf aufmerksam machen, dass in bestimmten fällen, insbesondere wenn dies aus gründen der politischen bedeutung erforderlich ist, der rat nicht daran gehindert ist, das europäische parlament freiwillig anzuhören. es sei auch darauf hingewiesen, dass mit dem energiegemeinschaftsvertrag hauptsächlich der besitzstand der gemeinschaft ausgeweitet wird, an dessen annahme das parlament ja umfassend beteiligt ist. lassen sie mich nun zum beschlussfassungsprozess in den gremien der energiegemeinschaft und zu dem von der europäischen gemeinschaft in diesen gremien einzunehmenden standpunkten kommen. wie sie wissen, besteht der institutionelle rahmen der energiegemeinschaft aus dem ministerrat, der ständigen hochrangigen gruppe und dem regulierungsausschuss. an dem mit den parteien des energiegemeinschaftsvertrags vereinbarten beschlussfassungsverfahren ist das europäische parlament nicht unmittelbar beteiligt. in artikel 52 dieses vertrags ist jedoch vorgesehen, dass der ministerrat dem europäischen parlament sowie den nationalen parlamenten der vertragsparteien jährlich einen bericht über die tätigkeiten der energiegemeinschaft vorzulegen hat. was den von der europäischen gemeinschaft in diesen gremien zu vertretenden standpunkt anbelangt, so wird dieser standpunkt gemäß artikel 4 des entwurfs eines beschlusses des rates über den abschluss des energiegemeinschaftsvertrags festgelegt und vom rat gemäß den einschlägigen bestimmungen des eg-vertrags angenommen. ein wichtiger aspekt dieses beschlussfassungsprozesses ist das erfordernis, dass die standpunkte der europäischen gemeinschaft zu beschlüssen der energiegemeinschaft, die unter die titel iii und iv des energiegemeinschaftsvertrags fallen, mit dem gemeinschaftlichen besitzstand im einklang stehen müssen. ausgenommen hiervon sind maßnahmen im rahmen des kapitels iv des titels iv des genannten vertrags, das die gegenseitige unterstützung bei unterbrechung der energieversorgung betrifft. was nun die beteiligung des europäischen parlaments anbelangt, so ist in absatz 5 von artikel 4 des entwurfs eines beschlusses des rates wie von der kommission vorgeschlagen festgelegt, dass das europäische parlament unverzüglich und vollständig über alle beschlüsse des rates zur festlegung von in den drei gremien des energiegemeinschaftsvertrags zu vertretenden gemeinschaftsstandpunkten zu unterrichten ist. eine ex-ante-unterrichtung des europäischen parlaments ist nicht förmlich festgelegt, jedoch hat der vorsitz die feste absicht, das parlament regelmäßig zu unterrichten. die kommission wird aufgefordert werden, dies ebenfalls zu tun. hinzu kommt – und dies wird der rat berücksichtigen –, dass der standpunkt, den das europäische parlament nach seiner unterrichtung einnimmt, sicherlich die künftige entscheidungsfindung der europäischen gemeinschaft beeinflussen wird. herr präsident! ich hoffe, dass mit diesen ausführungen nicht nur die fragen des verehrten abgeordneten beantwortet sind, sondern dass auch die sorge, dass member of the commission. mr president, before answering the questions put to me, i would like to start by explaining the global approach towards the energy community. we know, and there is some consensus, that the two main routes for enhancing energy security in the european union are diversification and the strengthening of market forces. extensions of the eu’s own market to include our neighbours would gradually create around the eu a shared regulatory area with common trade, transit and environmental rules. in this context, i thank you for giving me the opportunity to present a successful initiative in the region of south-east europe. it is not only because of its needs that the european union acted in this area. the disintegration of the former yugoslav energy system has brought havoc to the regional market, by breaking electricity connections, disrupting trade routes and forcing the system to work – on a chronic basis – far beyond its capacity. on the other hand, industrial decline and population shifts have made demand much more capricious and more varied, so the technical challenges of keeping the system alive were preventing development and a fresh start. indeed, some european union aid was being used to buy electricity and fuel oil for immediate consumption. such a situation could not go on. apart from these immediate needs, the commission made a strategic decision to look at the long-term needs, to gather international consensus for a way forward and create a real basis for post-war cooperation in the region. today, i can present to the european parliament the results of our joint work. it is valuable to the stabilisation and economic development of these countries. within ten years we have gone from war to cooperative management of the most essential sector of the economy: energy. along the way we have faced difficulties and sometimes scepticism. and i have to thank parliament for assisting us in overcoming these difficulties. i would like to thank in particular the rapporteur, mr chichester, and the shadow rapporteurs. the issues we have been discussing are not only related to investments. we have also addressed environmental and social issues in our debate. so the creation of the energy community for south-east europe clearly responds to the needs of the region and of the whole eu. let me now turn to the question. firstly, the energy community treaty provides for a procedure ensuring cooperation and mutual assistance of the parties in the event of disruption of gas or electricity supply affecting a party. this is quite an important clause. one example is the recent gas crisis between russia and ukraine, but also, for instance, the blackout in italy in 2003, which demonstrated the need for solidarity among european countries, and the importance and the benefits that such a solidarity clause could have in the energy sector. i would also recall that this winter serbia’s gas supplies were cut off for quite a considerable time. pursuant to the draft conclusion decision, the positions that can be taken by the european community under title iv of the energy community treaty, providing for the creation of a single energy market between the european community and the countries of south-east europe and containing the mutual assistance clause, have to be inspired by the existing acquis communautaire. as mutual assistance may not be fully covered by the existing acquis – and in some cases our acquis is perhaps not ambitious enough – it was important to introduce some flexibility to this limitation as regards the mutual assistance clause. the reference to specific circumstances allows for this flexibility. it will, ultimately, be up to the council to decide by qualified majority, whether or not the specific circumstances are met on a case-by-case basis. in my view, this concerns situations of extreme gravity and extreme disruption. of course any measure concerning the mutual assistance clause will have to remain within the external competence of the european community. let me highlight, in that regard, that decisions of the energy community on mutual assistance have to be taken by unanimity so that the european community will have a veto on all decisions to be adopted. secondly, let me stress that, through its proposal to the council, the commission has steadily acted in favour of an increased role of parliament as regards the ratification of the energy community treaty. in this regard, once the treaty has entered into force, i consider it of utmost importance that parliament be fully informed in advance of important decisions to be adopted by the energy community. to this effect, parliament will be informed in advance of each semi-annual ministerial council of the european energy community. i have also instructed my services to ensure that parliament is informed in advance of the european community position to be taken before the institutions of the energy community on important issues and that it has full access to the energy community’s documents. there are no restrictions on official documents of the energy community and all policy documents are placed on the energy community website. these documents are accessible to all those who have an interest in them. in addition, as provided for in the treaty, the energy community’s ministerial council will, on an annual basis, submit a report on the activities of the energy community to the european parliament and all other national parliaments involved, as the president-in-office mentioned. in line with the proposed conclusion decisions, the commission will further submit to parliament, every three years, a report on the energy community. i hope that my answers to the questions are satisfactory. i would also like to mention the issues referred to by the honourable member with regard to kozloduy, because i would like to separate this issue from the energy community treaty. the energy chapter with bulgaria was closed in 2002 and both sides have agreed to close that chapter on the basis that units 3 and 4 of kozloduy will be closed on the grounds of safety requirements. that means we have provided aid for bulgaria to deal with this situation. so i would not make a connection between these two issues, because the decisions have been taken by mutual understanding and we have done quite substantial work to help bulgaria deal with the consequences of the closure of units 3 and 4 of the kozloduy power station.

mr. chairman, please! natural disasters such as floods or droughts often affect regions in more than one member state. the european union must therefore act together, both in preventing and in remedying the consequences of disasters. the solidarity fund should therefore have a wider scope than before, allowing it to respond to crises resulting from natural disasters as well as those caused by industrial and technological disasters or acts of terrorism. it is also necessary to develop a european strategy for combating the effects of natural disasters, together with the appropriate community instruments for prevention, to adapt the use of the structural funds to disaster prevention and to coordinate closely with other community instruments. by ensuring the necessary flexibility in the allocation of available resources from the different funds, their operational capacity in the event of a disaster can be increased. in addition, individual member states and the community institutions must put particular emphasis on improving the existing early warning systems to minimise the impact of disasters, since even the largest solidarity fund, let alone the one we will have in the next 7 years, will not be able to cover all the losses that european union citizens suffer each year as a result of unforeseen disasters and catastrophes.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the belgian initiative of 2004 is a response to a series of sexual offences committed by michel fourniret. the fourniret case demonstrated that a person convicted in one member state for such an offence can subsequently move to another member state and there carry out work without any obstacles that allows him to have constant contact with children. the current framework decision on the recognition and enforcement in the european union of the prohibitions on convictions for sexual offences against children, as set out in the 2003 framework decision, addresses these legal loopholes. the proposal aims to ensure that a judicial ban on working with children following a conviction for sexual offences or child pornography is not only valid in the country where it was imposed, but in any other eu country to which the person subject to the ban is transferred. the proposed framework decision introduces the following:- obliges the member states where the convicted person resides to recognise the injunction issued in another country and to enforce it in their territory;- introduces the obligation to enter in the convicted person's register any injunction issued against a convicted person for sexual offences against children, including those issued by other states;- provides for the obligation to notify another state of the injunction when transmitting other information from the convicted person's register in accordance with applicable international and union law on legal aid in criminal matters;- obliges the member state whose convicted person's register is consulted in respect of the convicted person's past to always submit the information from the convicted person's register to the member state of which the person is a national in such a situation. the proposed modifications to the draft framework decision include, in particular: first, the extension of the definition of prohibition to include prohibitions on the performance of activities of any kind in public or private institutions dealing with the supervision of children or working with children. the idea is that not only educators or teachers who are going to work with children are bound by this ban, but also technical staff who may be employed in such institutions. secondly, to extend the protection of european union citizens by requiring member states to register convicted persons also for the prohibitions imposed in non-eu countries and to regulate situations of dual nationality. finally, it should be stressed that the proposed framework decision is a reflection of the implementation of the tampere european council conclusions of 1999, which stated that mutual recognition of judgments in criminal matters will be the cornerstone of judicial cooperation within the european union. we realize that there are no perfect solutions, but i am convinced that the successful implementation of this decision will significantly improve the safety of our children. however, the work on the problem of combating paedophilia cannot be completed with this document. member states must go further in implementing and enforcing the law on professional ineligibility. consequently, every employing institution should require that each person be screened for sexual offences against children.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i would like to thank mr. seeber for his work. i'm glad you did. today in this room, we talked about groundwater as the most important natural resource. we have to protect it from contamination. and now we're debating how we can protect ourselves from the destructive effects of water as an element, which is flooding. the need for close cooperation between the eu and non-eu countries in this area should be emphasised. of course, the principles of subsidiarity and flexibility must not be violated here. however, i believe that some unification is needed covering both the legal provisions and the principles of crisis management in the event of flooding, as well as ensuring full compatibility of rescue equipment. this will allow for rapid and coordinated assistance, which is very important in river basins that span several countries. the rapporteur rightly places a strong emphasis on flood prevention and the necessary protection and warning systems. in addition, adequate preparation of the population in the affected areas is needed, including through school education and a well-functioning civil defence system. in poland, where we also experienced flood damage this year in the carpathian basin and in lesser poland, volunteer fire brigades have been making a very serious contribution to rescue operations for many years - for which i would like to publicly thank them from this place. i would like to join those who see the negative impact of imprudent management of agricultural land, careless logging, the construction of housing estates in floodplains, and so on. for, note that only some natural disasters, including floods, are caused by forces of nature that are independent of man. yet, many of these disasters, often resulting in death, injury, and extensive damage, are the result of human irresponsibility or negligence. so let's be smart before we do any damage and minimize the losses. the directive we are debating is intended to help this, and hopefully it will be effective.
mr. chairman, please! the european parliament and council directives on flood risk assessment and management are documents on phenomena that have been known for centuries. watercourses are changing as a result of river regulation, agricultural activities, deforestation and forest loss, and therefore training is needed to prepare for floods that could reduce the impact and risk. where we have dams, we have levees, we have folders, we have no water barriers, we have much less damage from the floods of the century. the roads were not destroyed, as long as there were high passes and high bridges. flood control programmes at the level of the catchment areas of municipalities, counties and regions of the european union should be carried out with great imagination and take advantage of existing experience. all these activities support the directives. i'd like to thank mr. richard seeber for his job.
mr president, this directive is an important step for the security of europe. in july 1997, poland suffered its worst flood in 200 years, with 2% of the country's land area inundated. the disaster caused enormous economic, social and moral damage - 55 people were killed, and several hundred thousand homes, factories, sewage treatment plants, schools, and historic sites were destroyed. the flood losses were estimated at pln 13 billion, i.e. about eur 3 billion. then floods swept across europe. the draft directive stresses that the highest priority of the plan is the protection of human life. between 1997 and 2005, more than 700 people died in europe as a result of floods. this should include the costs of economic damage, farm flooding, road, environmental damage due to chemical pollution, flooding of landfills, soil erosion. the current directive contains specific measures to minimise the damage caused by floods. however, ecological and environmental effects should be taken into account. in many parts of the european union, the flood restoration efforts have caused serious and irreversible damage to river fauna and forests. hydrotechnical works were carried out using techniques that irreversibly upset the balance in the river and forest ecosystems. so there is a need to give serious thought to ways of rebuilding flood-damaged areas in a way that preserves the ecological balance rather than destroys it.
mr. chairman, please! the document we are discussing today is certainly needed, as it deals with the issues of flood risk assessment and management. this is all the more so as floods are and will be the most frequent type of natural disaster due to climate change, but they can also occur as a result of the opening of water reservoirs by neighbouring countries. a delayed response, or lack thereof, can cause the collected rivers to overflow, causing environmental damage, property damage, and even death. heavy rains can also cause river floods, especially in central and northern europe, in some cross-border areas. however, the directive, written in this way, gives the impression that floods will be a predictable and controlled phenomenon within the union, as they will be managed by a group of experts. however, there is no indication of a problem of flooding in peripheral areas. in poland, the eastern border is also the external border of the european union with belarus and ukraine, running along the bug river. it is difficult to imagine coordination of actions such as the polish-belarusian rescue or cooperation within the river basin with the involvement of all relevant authorities. the even more difficult task is to link all the financial strategies and mechanisms, especially cohesion policy, to a rational policy aimed at eliminating or reducing the risk of flooding. on the western side of the bug, union experts, authorities, crisis management teams using risk maps and legal instruments, or financial expertise, may be able to ensure that the flood is controlled and calm, with no losses. however, a few metres further on, close to the eu border, in belarus or ukraine, the flooding of further human settlements and industrial plants can be very violent, completely uncontrolled and lead to environmental hazards. such a scenario is obviously contrary to the laws of nature, because natural disasters, and they are undoubtedly floods, do not know political boundaries. in the drafting of the directive, greater attention should be paid to cross-border areas with third countries, such as ukraine and belarus in the case of poland. this is a real danger of human and economic loss, and pollution of my country's environment, but also of other countries bordering on it. of course, flexibility is needed, especially in the case of the regulations implemented in the member states and the reduction of red tape.
member of the commission. mr president, i should like to briefly describe the commission's views on a number of important issues raised by parliament. i would like to stress that most of the amendments adopted by the european parliament provide useful clarifications of the proposal and improve coherence, particularly with regard to the water framework directive. i would like to begin by commenting on the amendments which the commission can accept in their entirety, in principle or in part. floods and the risk management measures applied to deal with them have two aspects: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is not damaged. the commission therefore agrees with the rapporteur that it is important to strike the right balance between flood risk management measures and environmental protection, while maintaining adequate references to the water framework directive. the commission therefore accepts the following amendments: amendment no 36 on the assessment of existing artificial flood protection infrastructure, amendment no 60 on the economic and environmental assessment of flood management measures and amendment no 74 on the priority of measures for the sustainable management of flood risk. as regards the impact of climate change, the commission agrees that this should be taken into account, in particular when reviewing flood risk assessments. the commission can therefore accept amendments nos 38 and 73, which strengthen the relevant provisions of the directive. the commission does not wish to impose an unnecessary administrative burden on the member states and shares the view that the member states should, during the first period of application of the directive, be able to use existing maps and diagrams which meet the requirements of the directive. this was emphasized by the commission in recital 13 of the proposal, so the commission can accept in principle the amendments proposed by parliament, namely amendments nos 37, 55 and 71. effective and efficient implementation of the directive requires cooperation and coordination between the main flood risk management bodies in watersheds that cross administrative and political borders of several countries. the commission can therefore accept as a whole or in principle a number of amendments which further clarify these obligations. i could mention amendment no 62 in its entirety and amendment no 61 in principle. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. firstly, the commission considers that citizens have the right to protection against floods of any origin. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not affected by the floods. nor should the information necessary for their mapping be restricted. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 14, 27, 42, 43 and 47. in this context, amendment no 51 is also inadmissible because it is not in line with the rest of the directive. secondly, some amendments add unnecessary references or overlap with other elements of community legislation or create legal ambiguity. i refer in particular to amendments nos 53, 59 and 63. the commission cannot accept them. finally, the commission cannot accept amendment no 23, which seeks to remove the recital in the preamble to the charter of fundamental rights. the commission can accept 14 of the 20 new amendments, either in part or in full. i would like to refer to one particular amendment which cannot be accepted for very important reasons. this is amendment no 81, which proposes a derogation for national river basins under certain conditions. there are two reasons: firstly, the commission proposal applies to all watersheds, national and international. both citizens and businesses require the same level of flood risk protection and management, regardless of the type or geographical location of the water catchment area. any attempt to limit the scope of the directive to national water catchment areas would create discriminatory situations and set an undesirable precedent in the environmental policy of the european union. secondly, in terms of legal clarity, i have already mentioned that the commission supports a number of amendments which set out the conditions for the transitional phase to be used in a way that is compatible with the directive. amendment no 81 runs counter to this objective and creates legal uncertainty for citizens. in conclusion, mr president, i am pleased to announce that the commission accepts 71 amendments, 16 of which are in full and 55 in principle or in part. for the reasons i have mentioned, the commission cannot accept 24 amendments. i shall be submitting to the secretariat of parliament a full list of the commission's positions on the amendments. i would like to congratulate mr seeber once again on his efforts and his excellent work.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on tuesday at 12 noon. annex position of the commission

proponents and opponents of embryonic stem cell research. for example, introducing a so-called cut-off date that would make human embryonic stem cell lines eligible or not eligible for community funds would have far-reaching consequences. such a cut-off date has no scientific or objective basis. it might prevent the european researchers from using the lines they have created and force them to work recently produced. it might unduly limit access to the specific stem cell lines which are indispensable for patients. in other words, it has to be clear that any date will compromise the label of scientific excellence in this sector which i am personally eager to attach to this seventh framework programme, as long as ethical concerns are taken fully into consideration, which i believe is entirely the case with our proposal. one last word on subsidiarity: the current strict procedures and limitations on embryonic stem cell research entirely respect the subsidiarity principle. relying member of the commission. the commission’s competition enforcement priorities in the pharmaceutical sector have two key objectives: one is to tackle intra-brand competition between the producers of patented prescription products and the parallel importers of those products; the other is to promote competition in innovation for patented medicines between the pharmaceutical producers, which has declined in europe in the last decade, and to encourage intra-brand competition from generic substitutes after patent expiry. that should, in time, contribute to ensuring a wider choice of both patented and generic pharmaceutical products to european patients at affordable prices. due account is taken of the need for the industry to recover its research and development costs, given the industry’s heavy dependence on innovation for its further competitiveness. in that context, the honourable member can be assured that the commission is not circumspect about rigorously applying the anti-monopoly provisions in the pharmaceutical sector, for generic competition is an area which has suffered from under-enforcement in the past. however, the importance of the generic segment for the provision of affordable medicines in the enlarged union cannot be ignored. that is why the commission will give greater priority to competition in the generic sector in the immediate future. on the issue of parallel trade, the commission has always taken an active approach to combating restrictions on parallel trade in pharmaceuticals. in the commission’s opinion, parallel imports are a legal form of trade between the member states, constituting an alternative means of supply in the import countries. the commission is aware of the supply quota systems put in place by several pharmaceutical companies. under those systems, pharmaceutical companies unilaterally allocate a quota of medicines to their wholesalers. in principle the quota covers domestic demand for the medicines in question in a particular member state. the european courts have held that such unilateral supply quota systems are not within the scope of article 81 of the ec treaty when there is not enough evidence that they are the result of an agreement with wholesalers. however, another type of practice aimed at curbing parallel trade such as ‘dual pricing systems’ – which, as you know, are systems where prices differ according to whether the product is for local consumption or for export to the other member states – has been held to infringe article 81 in, for example, the glaxo-wellcome decision of may 2001. the greek national competition authority has initiated proceedings against restrictions on parallel trade on the basis of article 82, which prohibits the abuse of a dominant position. there are also parallel civil litigation proceedings pending in greece, dealing with the same matter. the commission is monitoring these developments closely. article 152 makes clear that the organisation and the delivery of health services and medical care are the responsibility of the member states. the competent national authorities are free to make their own decisions on pricing and reimbursement for pharmaceuticals, provided that these decisions are made in a transparent manner and do not create barriers to trade. the commission understands that in poland the price of reimbursable pharmaceuticals is subject to a ministry of health decision following representations from the industry. in discharging that duty, the polish authorities could and do use prices in other eu member states – including low-price countries – as a reference point. it should also be noted that the commission has recently launched a project under the pharmaceutical forum, which addresses the issue of national pricing and reimbursement practices. that project will take account of the interests of patients, member states, wholesalers, manufacturers and other stakeholders.

the next item is the report drawn up by mr giuseppe gargani on behalf of the committee on legal affairs on the effects of the judgment of the court of justice of 13 september 2005 (c-176/03 commission v council) [2006/2007 (ini)) ] (a6-0172/2006).
mr. chairman, please! the establishment of a single legal system based on common values and on the principle of the primacy of community law and close cooperation between the member states and the european institutions is paramount to the proper functioning of the single internal market of the european union. any action aimed at ensuring the effective functioning of community law stemming from the first pillar should be supported. the first community pillar is the only one that allows european legislation to be adopted in a democratic manner and ensures adequate judicial control. the judgment of the court of justice of 13 september is of great importance for the future development of community law. the court held that the precise definition of the legal basis of a measure must refer to the object and content of the measure itself, and therefore the decision on environmental protection, which wrongly identified the basis as the third pillar rather than the first, was annulled. in the light of that judgment, ongoing legislative initiatives whose legal basis may be considered to be erroneous should be withdrawn or modified. in addition, the possibility of initiating the legislative procedure on new legal bases for acts adopted under the third pillar, which according to the judgment can be considered to be wrongly based, should be considered. the tribunal's conclusion should not, however, be automatically extended to every possible area covered by the first pillar. it should therefore apply to areas falling within the community's basic principles, objectives and competences and individual cases should be examined on a case-by-case basis in close cooperation between the commission, the council and the european parliament. the member states are principally responsible for the proper application of community law. therefore, the conditions for including criminal law provisions in the first pillar should be clear and pre-defined.
mr. chairman, please! the council's framework decision on the protection of the environment through criminal law was intended to respond to the worrying increase in environmental crime, and this intention is to be commended. but the way in which the council has done this is not to be commended, because it has led to a dispute, and a double dispute. the first is institutional in nature and, since the treaties in force do not clearly and intelligibly define who is to do what in the union, there is therefore no clear division of competences between the union's institutions, and in particular between the council, the member states and parliament. the second aspect of the dispute concerns the legal basis relied on by the council in adopting the contested decision, wrongly relying on pillar iii, whereas the matter in question does not fall within pillar iii but within the community's competence in the field of environmental protection. therefore, the council of the european union had no right to take the above decision. by that decision, the council encroached on the competences conferred on the community by the community treaty and infringed the treaty on european union, which gives priority to those competences. moreover, by choosing the wrong legal basis, the council has deprived the european parliament of any influence on matters relating to environmental protection, which are clearly of a community nature and fall within its competence. i am sure that if the european union had a constitution, which defines the limits of competence, which defines who does what in the european union, there would be no dispute. we would have a clear law and the european court of justice would not have to intervene.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on wednesday at 12.30 p.m.

member of the commission. mr president, for the record i wish to confirm that the commission accepts all amendments that reflect the agreement allowing the adoption of this proposal in a single reading. i have arranged for a list of the commission’s position on all amendments to be handed to the secretariat for inclusion in the recordcommission’s position on amendments by parliament: see annex.. some members raised subjects this evening that are reflected in amendments that the commission is not in a position to accept and these relate to the following. a threshold of 1000 euros or dollars for incoming transfers would deprive authorities in charge of fighting money laundering and terrorist financing of an effective means to do their job. below the threshold, information on the payers would not have to be collected or recorded. the risk is that these funds could be used for financing new terrorist attacks. terrorist acts can be organised with little money. it has been estimated that the cost of the madrid attacks only amounted to about eur 8000 and any threshold for incoming transfers can easily be abused by dividing the amount to be transferred into several payments below the threshold. the general sunset clause that would limit the applicability of this regulation in time: this was not accepted by the council either. such a clause could be useful in certain cases in the context of better regulation, but the commission does not see added value in including this general clause in this regulation. inserting this clause would mean that users and providers of payment services would be deprived of the necessary legal certainty. a comprehensive review clause is no doubt better suited for this regulation. if it turns out in the light of the review that changes are needed, the commission will set them in motion and i therefore appeal to the house to accept this sensible solution. the comitology procedure under the provisions of this regulation covers a special procedure of authorisation by the commission for member states to conclude bilateral agreements with territories or countries outside the community. member states authorised to include such agreements will benefit from derogations from the obligations under the regulation. such waivers will allow member states to treat transfers of funds between that country or territory and the member state concerned as transfers of funds within the member state. amendment 103 limits in time, until 1 april 2008, the possibility for the commission to grant such authorisations. imposing such a sunset clause is clearly not in line with the recent agreement on the revised comitology procedure. as part of this deal both the council and parliament agreed not to limit in time the powers granted to the commission. for the same reasons, amendments 20, 22 and 24 are not acceptable either. some of you have raised the swift crisis widely reported in the media during the last few weeks. you are aware that the issue is on parliament’s agenda later this week and my colleague mr frattini will make a declaration on behalf of the commission. we will make sure assessment. no problems were detected on data protection issues. let me stress once more that non-compliance by 1 january 2007 with the agreed international standards to ensure an effective fight against the financing of terrorism will not only send a negative message to the financial community on europe’s commitment to fight terrorism. non-compliance would also have significant economic consequences due to disruption of money flows from and to the european union. the commission has been ready to take the concerns on board. the compromise found is a good one. it will make europe a
