the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. this own-initiative report on recent developments and prospects in the field of company law is intended to respond to the above actions of the commission and to develop parliament's strategic plans for further action in the field of company law. significant progress has been made in implementing the 2003 action plan. however, further action is needed to: achieve the objectives set out in the revised lisbon strategy; commit to growth and jobs; strengthen and increase industrial competitiveness; improve the business environment; and commit to supporting the social europe project. calls on the commission to ensure that the steps taken to modernise the area of company law and corporate governance are and will be consistent with the rules in related sectors, and stresses the importance of taking into account the case law of the court of justice of the european communities on the principle of freedom of establishment; parliament called on the commission to take account of the european social model, in particular the involvement of workers, when deciding on further measures to develop company law. better regulation and simplification are very important to increase the coherence and clarity of community legislation, especially in the area of company law, but should not be the only objective. the first step is to identify the areas where further initiatives at european union level are necessary to achieve the objectives. it is necessary to examine whether there is a need for a comprehensive consolidation of company law in a single legal act or whether, in the first stage, consolidation should cover only certain areas of company law. the commission's withdrawal of projects in areas where it should already have seen interest from the companies involved cannot be justified by the need for better regulation. the european parliament should be continuously involved in the process of developing, defining and adopting simplification measures. the european corporate governance framework should create the right institutional conditions to support the long-term profitability and employment prospects of companies, provide mechanisms to prevent mismanagement and guarantee transparency, accountability for investment and revenue. it should also be borne in mind that employees are a kind of human capital of the enterprise, and that employees are not only parties to the employment contract, but are also investors and citizens of the european union. employees should be seen, like shareholders, as persons involved in the company in the sense that they bear the risks associated with decisions concerning the company. the european parliament also calls on the commission to take greater account of the needs of smes in future legislative proposals or in future revisions of existing legislation, recalling that they are job creators and drivers of economic growth. in the field of company law, parliament welcomes the commission's proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the exercise of voting rights by shareholders of companies incorporated in a member state and whose shares are admitted to trading on a regulated market. the european parliament also welcomes the agreement reached on the proposals for a parliament and council directive amending the directive on the formation of public limited liability companies and on the maintenance and alteration of the capital of such companies, and the proposal for a parliament and council directive amending the directive on the annual accounts and consolidated accounts of certain types of companies. parliament should be continuously involved in the debate on further priorities in company law and corporate governance, which means, inter alia, that parliament will be regularly informed of discussions in expert groups. the european parliament's main expectations from the commission in the field of company law are: first, that the commission gives companies guarantees to choose between different management systems, including the monopolistic and dualistic system, without the need to adopt rules defining the powers and obligations of the company's management bodies; second, that it analyses the possibilities of changing the rules in the statute of the european company on the creation of such companies in order to simplify them and adapt them to market requirements; and third, that it submits a proposal for a private european company to meet the needs of small and medium-sized enterprises. the european parliament strongly condemns the fact that the commission has already decided to withdraw two proposals: the proposal for a regulation on the statute for a european company association and the proposal for a regulation on the statute for a european mutual company, as well as two proposals for directives supplementing these statutes with regard to employee participation. however, we note that in the commission's 2003 action plan, the commission announced its intention to actively support the legislative process undertaken in connection with these statutes. we call on the commission to present new drafts on the statutes of european mutual societies and on the statutes of european associations. the european parliament also calls on the commission to present in the near future a proposal for a 14th directive on the transfer abroad of the registered office of a limited liability company. the european parliament expects the commission to table a legislative proposal on the 'one share, one vote' principle only after the results of the revision of the parliament and council directive on takeover bids. in conclusion, i would like to the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. today marks the end of the legislative work on the package of regulations relating to cohesion policy for 2007-2013. we all remember the heated debate on the role and significance of cohesion policy in the european union, which is implementing the lisbon strategy, and the attempts to gradually reduce cohesion policy and even renationalize it. today we are discussing these facts in historical terms, but it is worthwhile, here in the european parliament, to keep reminding that the implementation of the principle of solidarity through, inter alia, cohesion policy is a permanent part of the functioning of the european union. its forms may change, adapted to new purposes, but to challenge it is to deny the basis on which the community functions. implementing cohesion policy therefore involves not only allocating funds and determining how they are used, but above all setting its actual objectives. adaptation of methods and means of implementation and subsequent practical implementation of the activities. in accordance with the treaty provisions, the policy of social and economic cohesion can be implemented with the help of common financial resources, but also without their participation, through joint actions in different member states aimed at similar objectives. the implementation of joint actions that go beyond national borders is covered by the interreg community initiative, which covers cross-border, transnational and interregional cooperation, in the current programming period. experience with interregion has shown that crossborder initiatives undertaken jointly by local and regional authorities from several member states are of great importance to them, create networks of cooperation and build mutual trust. these are therefore activities which, with a small amount of funding, create a very high added value. the new programming period should build on these positive experiences and, therefore, on the one hand, the typical interreg actions have been integrated into the mainstream of cohesion policy under objective iii and, on the other, the need has arisen to create new legal and organisational opportunities for the cooperation partners. hence the innovative idea of creating a new legal instrument that would be helpful in all types of cross-border, transnational and interregional activities. the initiative also aims to give cooperation partners, who do not always use european funds, a tool to help them organise various activities, including public services of a cross-border nature. according to the proposed regulation, public authorities and public entities created with their participation, i.e. governmental, regional and local authorities, will be able to sign an agreement within the european union, known as a convention, to register the new institution as a european grouping of territorial cooperation and to acquire legal personality for it, after agreeing on the objectives and principles of cooperation. a european grouping of territorial cooperation with legal personality would be recognised throughout the european union after notification to all member states. the new regulation introduces a new legal entity, which is why it has been met with many comments, doubts and even protests when dealing with systemic issues. the work on the regulation has been an example of consistent compromise, requiring repeated concessions and difficult decisions. it is worth noting that a solution has been developed which guarantees full control by the member states over the establishment and operation of the egtc. the compromise reached did not alter the nature of the new solution or its innovative form. today's vote is the culmination of legislative work, the opening up of new possibilities, but above all it is a form of appreciation for all those who have been building truly european, decentralised international cooperation for many years. as a rapporteur member from a country which became a member of the european union in the last enlargement, i had the opportunity to learn about the complexities of the legislative process and therefore i would like to thank in particular for the very constructive and positive cooperation, in particular commissioner danuta hübner, the representatives of the directorate-general for regional policy (dg regio), the representatives of the successive presidencies, in particular the austrian presidency, the secretariat of the committee on regional development and the political advisers, as well as my polish colleagues and experts.

author of the draft opinion of the committee on employment and social affairs. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. in preparing the opinion on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs on the draft council regulation laying down general rules for the european regional development fund, the european social fund and the cohesion fund, we proposed 32 recommendations for this document. in our opinion, we have focused primarily on the integration of the needs of disabled people in the implementation of projects financed by the structural funds. we also called for the criteria for eligibility under the regional competitiveness and employment objective to be extended to the level of education in the member state concerned. we also asked for the bureaucratic procedures for using the structural funds to be simplified, both by means of a larger amount of advance payments to beneficiaries at the start of the implementation of operational programmes and by maintaining the so-called multi-fund system, i.e. the possibility of financing programmes not from just one but from a larger number of funds. we also proposed a slight distinction between reporting and reporting rigidity, believing that excessive bureaucracy does not serve the efficient use of european funds, which are the basis for the development of many regions. not all our recommendations have, of course, been accepted, but that is the logic of parliamentary work and compromise which underlies decisions in a community as diverse as the european union. but we're very happy with the way this collaboration turned out. they particularly welcome the solutions for disabled people, social and non-governmental organisations, but also the very sensible proposals on the issue of recognising vat as an eligible cost for certain activities. in view of all this, i join mr hatzidakis in his request that the proposed regulation be put to the vote.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. record profits on the one hand, closures and relocations of businesses on the other. and many people in the eu today are faced with the same fearful question every day: when does it affect me, when does it affect my workplace, when is it my turn? in the process of transformation in central and eastern europe, entire economies have collapsed and millions of jobs have disappeared. but people understood that this was the result of communist mismanagement. but many people are baffled by what is happening in some industries in the old eu countries: textiles, footwear, furniture, household appliances, pharmaceuticals and cars - sectors that were previously considered safe are now in turmoil. few people are prepared for the structural change we are witnessing. it is therefore high time to help the many who have lost their bearings to find them again. the importance of today's discussion goes far beyond the possible closure of an automobile plant in portugal. it is a debate on the future of work in europe. it is also time to state some truths clearly: firstly, we are in a new phase of competition and structural change will continue to accelerate. we must not turn a blind eye to this. competition is competition whether we want to play or not. the question is not whether we can survive the competition. the great social question of our time is how many life chances this competition will cost us, i.e. the great social question of our time is the question of the future of our jobs. and we need to face him. anyone who still believes that other issues are paramount does not understand the world of today and its challenges. we need more sustainable, environmentally sound growth, and we need more and better jobs - otherwise the social face of europe will become a cold and cynical face, a face that does not fit our european idea of life. this concept is based on the division of responsibility between the individual and society. it is based on solidarity, social equality and social cohesion. the keyword for the european society of the 21st century, which will offer people new opportunities for life, is competitiveness. we know that a fortress portugal, a fortress germany, a fortress poland or europe is not an option in the open world of the 21st century. we must face and lead open competition, and we must lead it to the top, to the best solution, the best technology, the highest standard. secondly, we have launched a common european policy for growth and employment. this policy must now be vigorously implemented - at european, national and regional levels - otherwise we will be faced with the prospect of further dismantling of our social model - in the form of closed factories and research laboratories that have moved away, because that too is already in place. i would caution against thinking that we can easily accept that production is going away, since research and development will remain with us. once production is gone, research and development will follow. a policy for growth and employment can only be a policy which offers favourable conditions for enterprises - i said enterprises. in the economy, in the companies, jobs are being created and in the companies, jobs are being lost. no order from any single member state or from the eu as a whole can change that in the slightest. but we can do one thing - we can have a policy that creates the external conditions to make it attractive for companies to do their jobs, to grow, to invest and to create jobs in europe. this is the meaning of the word 'business-friendly policy'. thirdly, an active industrial policy that keeps industry in europe is more necessary than ever. the idea that industry belongs in the museum of the world is as wrong as the idea that industry is the world's biggest polluter. i advise anyone who still thinks that way to member of the commission. mr president, i would like straightaway to thank mr schmidt for this report and for drawing attention to my increasingly conspicuous consumption habits, which, i am afraid, are becoming only too obvious as i grow into this job as europe’s trade commissioner. sincerely and warmly i would like to thank him for this report, which i think is very valuable and will be well received. fair trade is one of the key tools, in my view, to enhance sustainable development and to equip us better to fight poverty in the world, and as a concept it is developing fast. it is undoubtedly a very popular trade practice. it is gaining in currency and appeal with public opinion, and helps to raise public awareness about all the issues that are involved in sustainability. you are not just undertaking an act of consumption that is good in terms of the content of what you consume. it is also a stimulus to the brain. it makes you think and therefore it is even more valuable. consumers do take into account considerations about the conditions of production. people care, they do not just eat, and fair trade has pioneered this in a most attractive way. the commission actively supports fair trade. we took on commitments to fair trade in the cotonou agreement with the acp countries, as well as in our communication on policy coherence for development. many trade and development assistance projects support fair trade: development projects to the tune of over eur 4 million in 2003, and growing. these consist mainly of support for ngo activities, but also of direct aid to the harmonisation of standards at work. we also participate in fair trade events. one could argue that whilst fair trade helps salve the conscience of those who buy such products, others continue, nonetheless, to exploit the needy. i am not happy about that argument: fair trade is not a panacea for all the problems of poor producers, nor does it necessarily mean that because you are not buying and consuming fair trade products you are exploiting the poor. what is required to tackle poverty and to enhance development is a general and coherent policy framework. it is this that we need to develop, to conceptualise, and this report will help us to do so. fair trade is private and limited to the participating producers, while the un millennium development goals are for all. so fair trade is particular and specific, the millennium development goals are general and wide-ranging; but there is a clear interconnection between the two. the objective is different for an individual and for eu policy-making. an individual makes a personal choice. he or she is entitled to exercise that choice. you cannot automatically translate that into a more wide-ranging policy. the individual consumer looks at one packet of coffee, rightly. policy-makers, on the other hand, have to take into account the sector as a whole and our obligations to that sector as a whole. we need a complete and public solution – one that should not be confined, therefore, to fair trade only. as the report rightly points out, there are other non-fair trade operators that can achieve similar results to those obtained by fair traders, that have the same growth potential and that can influence consumer choice and the international trading schemes. we should fully use the potential of all credible initiatives to support sustainability. that should be our test. does it help, does it aid, does it take forward sustainability? if it does, that should govern our response and attitude to it. building on commitments taken previously, we want to explore with our partners the use of economic partnership agreements with the acp countries, as well as other trade agreements, for including specific incentives targeted at improving market access for fair trade products. that is where i believe we can leverage our interest and leverage our commitment most beneficially. it is very useful, therefore, that the report points to the danger of inappropriate national legislation in the field of fair trade. i am aware of some initiatives being taken that might harm the status that fair trade has already achieved. we need to be vigilant about these and to see, therefore, whether it is not better to take a more coherent and collective approach in order to leverage the greatest benefits for fair trade. conversely, too firm an adhesion to the particular approach embodied in fair trade would be at risk of being discriminatory against other systems, some of them acknowledged in your report, which have similar claims and that we can and should support. you are right about the need to protect consumers, the question is how. i believe the role of policy is to ensure that messages given to consumers are accurate and transparent, and i am glad that this is also stressed in the report. we already have protection against misleading claims, but we might consider going further and help engage the consumer actively in the ethics of production. i believe that there is scope for better information about claims schemes in general, and work is in progress on this. i will ask my services to look at how sustainability is enhanced by different certification and assurance schemes, including fair trade. we will look at all the suggestions made in this report and of course keep parliament informed of further developments. we need a dialogue with parliament on a continuing basis. i am glad, therefore, that this report provides the framework, both for this dialogue and for the way in which we can, should and will take our commitment in this area further forward. in conclusion i would like to thank the rapporteur again for the quality of this report.

rapporteur. – mr president, the npi regulation is of major importance. it provides an essential basis for the european union’s work and partnership with our neighbouring countries to promote and assist political and economic reforms. today’s vote follows a lengthy process of negotiations on many detailed and complex issues, which all sides approached in a constructive spirit. i am pleased to report that many significant amendments proposed by parliament have been accepted. as a result, the regulation is more complete and more comprehensive. the amendments i have now tabled jointly with the shadow rapporteurs of the ppe-de and pse groups reflect the common intention to secure a first-reading agreement. the normal legal-linguistic verification process should deal with any remaining textual variations on this basis. there are minor textual variations in article 3.1 and in certain amendments. these are considered purely linguistic or technical and do not involve any point of substance.

on behalf of the ppe-de group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the resolution which the european parliament is to adopt today is in fact a resolution in defence of freedom of expression - the freedom of expression which is the foundation of any democratic society. it is safe to say that the internet is the best media outlet for protecting this freedom, but governments in many countries are trying to influence the content that is being shared online. legislative initiatives in many countries aim to regulate the flow of this wild and dangerous river that the internet can seem, and thus unfortunately carry a serious threat of restricting freedom of speech. after all, a personal computer with a printer is a potential printing press on which to print leaflets, letters, and even entire books for informal circulation. a computer connected to the internet is nothing more than a radio tuned to radio free europe, and an interactive radio in which anyone can speak and comment. this is a serious threat to any totalitarian state or state that restricts access to information to some degree. on the internet, you can only censor individual pages, you can't censor the entire web, but there is this temptation and threat to do so; for example, the chinese government has created an internet police force that checks whether any of the tens of millions of chinese internet users are violating the rules of using the web, and for such a violation, there is a penalty of up to ten years in a labor camp. internet café owners employ staff to monitor the user's screen for any unauthorized content, which is filtered by passwords. if you see the words "tibet" or "dissident" or "china and human rights" on the page, that page gets blocked. but the internet, with its anarchist nature, is actually a salt of the earth for governments and bureaucrats, and there's no shortage of them in the cradles of democracy in europe and the united states. it's important to remember that the eternal race between freedom and censorship never ends, but it's also an endless struggle between good and evil. we must remember that the freedom that the internet gives us also carries the threat of the distribution of anti-democratic and anti-moral content.

madam president! the commission proposal has two objectives: to improve the functioning of the internal market and to implement the community strategy for reducing co2 emissions from passenger cars. in order to be consistent with the union's environmental objectives and the kyoto protocol, co2 emissions should be significantly reduced to reach the community target of 120 grams of co2 per kilometre, and tax measures are a strong incentive for consumers. it should be stressed that the aim here is not to harmonise or to introduce new taxes. the commission has also proposed to extend the scope of the tax exemption to include the taxation of motor vehicles. the taxation of motor vehicles is highly diversified and uncoordinated across member states. a tax system where the amount of the registration tax is linked to co2 emissions is the right direction. this provides the basis for a longer-term approach to approximate the rates of road registration tax and to guarantee fair competition on the european market as a whole. the registration tax should be gradually reduced, which would help to eliminate the disparities in the european union car market. it is also necessary to establish a coherent and transparent system for the refund of registration duty based on clearly defined criteria. it is also important to ensure that the abolition of the registration tax is implemented in accordance with the principle of budgetary neutrality.
mr. chairman, please! a word of appreciation for taking up the subject. however, the emissions of cars are a function of the amount of fuel they burn, or mileage, and the quality of the gasoline, and in general a function of time. the proposed tax solution goes in two directions: abolishing the currently mandatory so-called registration fees and replacing them with a new tax paid upon purchase of the vehicle or annually. so the question is, what do the authors want? because the new tax is by definition unfair. it will be the same for the consumer who travels many kilometres and pollutes the air a lot, as well as for the one who does not drive much, as they say in poland, uses the car to go to church on sundays. moreover, the law imposes an obligation to pay the tax in advance, whereas the damage, or pollution, is caused in the distant future. moreover, the costs of the charges can and will be borne primarily by the poorest consumers, and will also worsen the conditions for the purchase of used cars. if so, then one can doubt whether the law is not written to order, with the interest of car companies in mind, who are looking for solutions that are beneficial to them in the face of stagnating demand. the more so because the new tax will pass through the hands of the corporations themselves, which will increase their revenues and increase their financial income. the authors also do not indicate the amount of the tax and there is a danger or concern as to the amount of revenue to the budgets of the member states. the programme we can support is as follows: the emission standards for new cars must be systematically tightened, the fuel quality standards must be tightened, taxes and charges on car purchases must be abolished. consideration should be given to introducing an environmental tax on fuel prices and to allocating the revenue thus obtained to research into new technologies and cleaner fuels. only such solutions will be beneficial in the long term for consumers, producers, environmentalists and the whole economy.

in writing. any violence, whether physical, psychological or sexual, constitutes a serious violation of the human right to life, security, liberty and dignity. the use of force against vulnerable people, such as children, young people and women, also poses a serious threat to their physical and mental health. the consequences of such actions are also very serious for the psychological and social development of families and communities. unfortunately, violence is still a daily reality in every member state of the european union. the collective actions and actions taken so far to speak out and prevent this often shameful or marginalized problem are timid first steps in the fight against violence. another programme, daphne iii, with a budget of €115 million, aims to prevent and combat violence in all its forms, in the private and public spheres. it aims to protect children, young people and women from violence by taking preventive measures and providing support and protection to any victims. for daphne to be effective, it must be visible to the public. in addition to actions such as supporting and assisting ngos, institutions, organisations and associations, it is necessary to carry out effective campaigns to raise public awareness of the problem of violence and in particular of trafficking in women and children for sexual exploitation. however, aid should not be understood as just ad hoc measures, but also, for example, to facilitate access to the labour market for victims of violence and thus to facilitate their smooth integration into society. in this light, the initiative to establish a european year against violence against women deserves strong support.
president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have the honour to present to you, on behalf of the presidency of the council, the draft general budget of the european communities for the financial year 2007, which was adopted by the council on 17 july 2006. this is the first budgetary procedure under the new financial framework. the transition to the new financial period should be smooth, while ensuring continuity and consistency. i believe that the budgetary authorities, the european parliament and the council, will continue to cooperate well in this respect. i am convinced that the two institutions share the same objective, namely to agree on the 2007 budget by the end of the year. before i go into more detail on the draft budget adopted by the council, i would like to recall the main principles which have guided the council's decision-making. first of all, i would like to stress that the council fully complied with the new interinstitutional agreement of 17 may 2006. the council thus reaffirmed its attachment to the principle of the general budgetary discipline at the eu level, in accordance with the national practice. particular attention was paid to respecting the annual ceilings for expenditure laid down in the new financial framework and to leaving sufficient room for manoeuvre in the ceilings for the various headings in the event of unforeseen circumstances. the assessment of precisely defined and real expenditure needs has been a central principle in our budgetary approach. the fact that all the priorities of the european union must be financed in sufficient quantities and in due time does not mean that the appropriations should be considered excessive. in order to ensure sound and disciplined financial management, the council has analysed in detail the needs of all the policy areas. after taking account of the previous implementation of the budget, a careful examination of selected operational reports, the capacity and actual needs for 2007, the council concluded that the increase in payment appropriations controlled in the draft budget was appropriate. the council considers that this level of payment appropriations is adequate and not too low. i would like to draw attention to the fact that the council has consistently followed a bottom-up approach. the final figures in our draft budget are therefore the result of targeted measures based on objective factors. the council's first reading is therefore by no means based on cross-line cuts. the above also applies to administration. secondly, we have taken a holistic approach. we have examined a number of commission activity-specific reports covering all the budgetary policy areas. thirdly, the eu budgetary procedure needs to be innovative. this is best achieved by an equal and active examination of the budgetary authority. without innovative budgetary solutions, we cannot promote the union's competitiveness and improve the efficiency of the institutions' governance. the total amount of commitments in this draft budget is eur 125.8 billion. the increase is 3.7% compared to the 2006 budget. the payment appropriations total eur 114.6 billion, which is 2.3% higher than in the 2006 budget. sub-heading 1a has seen little reduction in commitment appropriations, as the council attaches great importance to competitiveness and to responding to global challenges. the council also proposed two new pilot projects for this sub-heading, one on the learning triangle and the other on the union's own energy security. the council shall also adopt a statement on pilot projects and preparatory actions. the new interinstitutional agreement requires both budgetary authorities to present their intentions for pilot projects or preparatory actions. the council's proposal sets out four specific areas for priority action by the european union in which the council considers that pilot projects or preparatory actions should be carried out. i hope that by working together, we can reach a common vision. for subheading 1b, the council approved the commitment appropriations in accordance with the preliminary draft budget. the council reduced payment appropriations by eur 425 million in the budget lines for the completion of programmes started before 2000 and for the 2000-2006 programmes, taking account of the current level of implementation of these programmes. as regards the new programming period, the council did not make any reductions and also issued a statement expressing its concern that the commission should be able to adopt rapidly the operational programmes and projects submitted by the member states. in title 2, the council made a limited reduction of eur 365 million for all the budget lines for agricultural market interventions, except for those budget lines for which a special reduction of the same amount had already been made. these reductions follow the general principle of taking into account the previous rate of implementation and estimates of actual needs. however, the council noted that expenditure on agriculture and international fisheries agreements would be reviewed in the autumn on the basis of a letter of amendment from the commission. for commitment appropriations under subheading 3a, the council left a margin of eur 75 million. the council, however, increased the budget for the external borders fund, considering it an important political priority. the council increased the payment appropriations for heading 4 for crossborder cooperation and reconstruction in iraq because of their political importance. in accordance with the interinstitutional agreement, the council left a reserve of eur 220 million for commitments for unforeseen events. for the common foreign and security policy, the council approved the amount proposed in the preliminary draft budget, which also corresponds to the provisions of the interinstitutional agreement. in heading 5 on administrative expenditure, the council took a holistic view. it examined very carefully the budgetary needs of each institution. the increase in administrative expenditure is nevertheless 3,4% higher than in the 2006 budget. the increase in the council's administrative expenditure was limited to 0.3%, which is noteworthy. the council considers the recruitment of new staff to be of great importance in view of the 2004 enlargement and the enlargement to come. it has therefore approved all the new enlargement measures requested for 2007. one of the council's main objectives has been to ensure real productivity growth in the eu administration over the period covered by the new financial framework. to this end, the council adopted an opinion on a comprehensive programme to increase productivity in the administration for the period 2007-13. you know the different parts of the governance package very well. i would like to stress that this is an objective set by the council, not by any single member state or by the presidency alone. in the context of title 5, i would also like to recall the second council statement on the implementation of the recruitment process for the 2004 enlargement. the council is particularly concerned about the slowdown in recruitment this year. we expect significant progress in the recruitment process to be made as soon as possible in order to achieve the widest possible geographical balance. i would hope that parliament would support this endeavour and therefore the statement in question. my point of departure is that the modernisation requirements for the administration must also be applicable to the institutions of the union. the eu institutions are no different from other organisations. the eu must do its job as efficiently as possible. in this way we can show the public that we are really giving their money something back, something with added value. this requires the ability of budgetary authorities to prioritise resources. at the same time, improving the efficiency of administration increases citizens' confidence in the union's actions. in the coming months we will have to deal comprehensively with the crisis in the middle east and the necessary eu action. we must also not forget that, for the future, the european parliament and the council must address the global challenges facing the union in the 2007 budgetary procedure. finally, i am confident that we will achieve our main objective and that we will have a sufficient but not over-allocated budget in time for the financial year 2007. we know that this budgetary procedure is only in its early stages and that the final adoption of the 2007 budget is still a long way off. but i am confident that we will be able to explore all the possibilities to reach a final agreement that can be accepted by all the parties and above all by the citizens. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for your interest.
author of the draft opinion of the committee on budgets. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the work on the 2007 budget confirms the old truth that while there are repetitive procedures, there are no routine budgets. i would like to add a few words to those of our rapporteur, mr elles, to address some of the problems we face in 2007. the first is not the most important, because it is technical, analytical in nature, i.e. the problem of the comparability of annual budgets is reiterated. this is the budget for 27 countries. this problem of comparability "became acute" as the geography of the european union changed in 2004/2005, but it still exists and i agree with the view that without the separation of expenditure for bulgaria and romania there is no full comparability of annual budgets. the second question, the most serious, mr elles asked, is how much the first year of the new financial perspective should make us rethink, not so much the budgetary structure as the budgetary priorities; how much continuity and how much change will there be in this first year of the new financial perspective? i see a certain continuity on the council's part, namely, that the horizontal cuts are still being made, but this time more strongly supported by the so-called activity statements. i see the traditional preference for the common foreign and security policy, but i would like to emphasize that the rapporteur of parliament has a very strong mandate, both from the commission and from parliament as a whole, to verify the individual budget lines in terms of what is called a cost-benefit analysis. this is a very strong mandate and a very strong principle that will govern the first reading of the 2007 budget in parliament. this round of negotiations begins tomorrow, after we've agreed with the other committees, of course. there is the problem of 2007, as the problem of implementing a new generation of multiannual programmes based on new regulations, with new instruments for foreign trade. the question is: how much of the budgetary discrepancy justifies the careful budgeting for 2007, which is very clear on the payment side? that was probably the main reason why the starting point is so low this time. the payments already in the commission's initial draft are less than 1% of gross national income. the council made further cuts of €1 billion 757 million, creating an unusual margin between the 2007 budget and the ceilings set in the financial perspective for that year. in our view, this is an insufficient level of payments to finance the stated objectives of the european union, as is clear from the european union's ambitions as a global player, that is, in the international arena, in research and development funding. the implementation of the budget next year is also a question of quality and motivation of the administration, and in this context we look at and analyse the council's very rigorous approach to employment and skills in the european commission. we accept the commission's signal that the reduction of over eur 50 million in equipment will prevent recruitment, especially from the new member states. there mr. chairman, please! in a rapidly globalising world economy, it is absolutely crucial that europe develops cooperation with emerging economic powers such as china and india. however, this cooperation should be mutually beneficial. unfortunately, in the case of china-eu relations, this sound principle has been undermined to the detriment of europe. this is due to the following reasons. first, chinese producers do not include in the cost of production, inter alia, social security contributions for workers and environmental costs. this allows them to offer chinese products at significantly lower prices. secondly, the production of many exported products, such as metal products, in china benefits from various forms of state support, which is prohibited as public aid under eu rules. the export of these products to the european market thus creates unfair competition for european producers. third, the chinese currency is clearly overvalued against the dollar or the euro. the artificial maintenance of the current price clearly improves the efficiency of chinese exports and deteriorates the efficiency of imports to the chinese market. fourth, the chinese authorities have taken virtually no action to curb the massive counterfeiting of branded products by chinese producers. suffice it to say that as much as 70% of all counterfeit products detected on the european market originate from china. in this context, the european commission should do everything possible to minimise the phenomenon of unfair competition from china, in particular it should intensify the following actions. first, the commission should increase its pressure on china, both in the wto and directly, to eliminate unfair competition from china, in particular through exchange rate policy. secondly, the commission should adopt a coherent anti-dumping policy towards china as soon as possible. in particular, the commission should consider imposing high anti-dumping duties in the sectors entry into force of the new directive. i understand this to be the proposal tabled before this plenary. on amendments 46 and 82, i should provide some further clarification about the daily limit value of pm10. this protects sensitive individuals against the impact from short-term exposure to particles in the air. it is different from the annual limit value, which provides protection to all from long-term exposure. one cannot simply substitute a more stringent annual limit value for the daily limit. this is what the health experts say. the key to ensuring compliance with both daily and annual limits is to undertake good and timely air quality assessments and to take the necessary steps to reduce emissions. it is clear that many authorities have not done this and now they have compliance problems. on amendments 49 and 50, the proposed concentration cap for pm2.5 is set at a level consistent with the stringency of the annual limit value for pm10, which the commission is not proposing to change. it is also useful to remember that the commission has proposed two ways of tackling pm2.5: the concentration cap of 25 micrograms per cubic metre and the exposure-reduction approach, where average levels in urban areas will be reduced over ten years. these methods combined will work to deliver health improvements. our modelling work, which underpins the thematic strategy and the air quality proposal, shows that greater health improvements can be obtained by allowing the member states to choose where to reduce pollution levels. this is the aim of the exposure reduction targets. this flexibility will be limited if the concentration cap forces member states to divert resources to ensure compliance in some specific hotspot regions, where few health improvements may be available. for public health, a general reduction in exposure is preferable. in summary, on the air quality legislative proposal, i am pleased to say that the commission can support 32 amendments, in part or in principle. i shall give parliament’s secretariat a list detailing the commission’s position on the amendments commission’s position on amendments by parliament: see annex..

on behalf of the pse group. – mr president, while taking into account the current diversity of national judicial systems, it is highly desirable to promote mutual recognition of judgments between the european union member states. as already indicated by the tampere european council, the mutual recognition principle is the cornerstone of judicial cooperation in both civil and criminal matters. that being so, it is of the utmost importance to lay down an appropriate legal basis, so that a conviction handed down in one member state can be taken into account in new criminal proceedings against the same person concerning different facts in other member states. the commission proposal for a framework decision should be approved as amended. the object of the mutual recognition principle is to confer the same validity and the same effect on convictions handed down in other member states as on previous national convictions. it should be explicitly stated that the member state is not required to enforce the conviction handed down in another member state, but just to draw the appropriate conclusions from the earlier case in the new proceedings. furthermore, the effects of previous convictions will still be governed by national laws in each member state. a principle of assimilation of judgments given in other member states to national convictions should be established, still leaving it to national legislation to draw the appropriate conclusions from the principle. however, i have to consider it necessary for previous sentences to be taken into account, provided that their weight in the other evaluation is equal to the sentence issued by the member state in which proceedings have been opened. moreover, in the case of criminal proceedings in the member state, a firm conviction related to acts not punishable in that member state must not be taken into account.
mr. chairman, please! the framework decision we are debating today is extremely important in terms of assimilation combined with the harmonization of the law. i share the rapporteur's view that the only criterion for deciding whether and to what extent previous convictions handed down abroad should be given legal effect is national law. but we must not forget the basic principles of ne bis in idem, limitation or amnesty, or removal from the national criminal register. i therefore think that article 4 should be retained. it should also be stressed that we cannot allow judgments handed down abroad for acts which are not punishable in that member state to be taken into account in criminal proceedings in a member state. like the rapporteur, i believe that the best place for the provisions of article 6 is the proposal for a council framework decision on the organisation of the exchange of information from the register of convicted persons between member states and the contents thereof.

member of the commission. madam president, my colleague, commissioner mandelson, regrets not being able to be here for this very important debate, but he has had to travel to the united states for multilateral discussions. the european commission welcomes the report of the committee on women’s rights and gender equality. for the european union, the purpose of global governance is to make possible development that is socially, economically and environmentally sustainable. that is why we wish to promote policies that provide sustainable responses to gender-based issues, whether they are countries’ domestic policies in some cases backed by international aid, common policies such as those forming the building blocks of the european union, or international commitments. trade liberalisation has provided new opportunities for many women in developing countries, providing new employment and in many cases reducing the gender gap in wages, leading to greater empowerment and social standing of women in society. nonetheless, the rapid changes in national economies that can result from globalisation also provide challenges to policy-makers to ensure that the benefits and opportunities of globalisation are maximised and the short-term costs in certain sectors are minimised. the european commission believes that clear social conditions underpin sustainable productivity growth and promote the efficient production of high-quality goods and services generating a net added value. policies that mitigate the adverse effects of a changing economy on specific groups of people or regions, good social services and social protection accessible to all, social dialogue, the respect for fundamental social rights including core labour standards, minimum standards for working conditions and for ensuring workers’ upstream involvement in managing change – all these play a crucial role. the european commission promotes core labour rights in eu trade policy. core labour standards are defined by the ilo to include convention no 100 on equal remuneration for men and women workers for work of equal value, and convention no 111 on discrimination in the workplace. in the multilateral context, a reference to core labour standards was included in the declaration of the first world trade organization ministerial conference in singapore in 1996. regrettably, wto members did not agree to include this issue as part of the doha development agenda. nevertheless, the commission is committed to addressing trade and social development, core labour standards and commitment to meaningful dialogue between the wto and the international labour organization, both in the eu’s own trade policy review and the trade policy reviews of other countries. as part of this process, the international convention of free trade unions’ reports on core labour standards are prepared ahead of each trade policy review. the commission is also strongly in favour of observer status for the ilo in the wto. the european commission has also pursued social development objectives in regional, bi-regional and bilateral arrangements. all its most recent agreements recognise and promote social rights as part of the universal objective of decent work for all. the commission has, for example, entered into dialogue and cooperation with countries such as chile, south africa and bi-regionally with the acp countries, the gulf cooperation council, mercosur and other regions. the european commission remains of the view that the discussion and pursuit of social issues should not be used for protectionist purposes and it rejects any unilateral sanctions-based approach. the objective is to further social progress with a view to promoting benefits for all. since 1998 the ec has also been granting trade preferences under the generalised system of preferences, special incentive arrangements to those developing countries that assure the respect of the core labour rights as defined by the ilo and comply with international recognised standards on sustainable forest management. currently, some 180 developing countries and dependent territories are granted gsp. in the framework of the new gsp scheme, adopted on 27 june 2005 by the council, a gsp-plus initiative for sustainable development provides additional tariff preferences for countries that have signed and effectively implemented un and ilo conventions on human rights and labour rights, including those on gender equality. a total of 15 countries have ratified the core conventions and received gsp-plus status. a gender helpdesk currently operates under the relex family of the commission. the services of the gender helpdesk are part of a larger effort to build capacity and knowledge to promote gender equality and fully implement the strategy of gender mainstreaming. a tool kit has also been published to give practical help to commission staff on how to mainstream gender issues. the ec is also developing a close relationship with the international labour organization on trade-related matters aimed at promoting core labour standards through assessment, capacity-building and enforcement in developing countries. in 2005-2006 the commission has been funding an ilo pilot project aiming to develop decent work indicators in developing countries for examining the relationship between decent work and trade liberalisation. case studies have been undertaken in the philippines and uganda. the data gathered include disaggregated statistics on employment, wages and working hours for women and men. these data provide a more sophisticated picture of decent work than previously available. the commission will explore the potential to use these indicators in future aid programmes with developing countries to help them manage social adjustment to globalisation, and the report will be submitted to the european parliament. the european commission will also look into the potential for using decent work indicators as part of trade sustainability impact assessments.

member of the commission. mr president, i am here today to talk about the big issue of small technologies. over 2000 years ago, the ancient greek politician demosthenes said: ‘small opportunities are nanotechnology is already making a difference in many areas. for example, new medical treatments are being developed for severe diseases such as brain tumours and alzheimer’s disease; it is helping the environment through more efficient catalysts, better batteries and more efficient light sources; and smaller, lighter and better-performing materials, components and systems are being created. but nanotechnology could also make a huge contribution to major global challenges such as how to tackle threats to the environment, how to make better use of resources and create less waste, and how to improve energy generation technologies. europe is in a leading position in the world today, partly thanks to the commission’s framework programme. european industry should now reap the benefits of that knowledge through innovative products and processes. but to follow through, we need to take action on several fronts, which are outlined in the commission’s communication nanosciences and nanotechnologies: an action plan for europe 2005-09. these include the need to increase investment, boost interdisciplinarity, create necessary infrastructures, expand human resources and foster innovation. much progress has already been made in implementing the action plan: commission funding for research in nanosciences and nanotechnologies has steadily increased to about eur 470 million in 2005. in fact, the commission has now become the world’s largest single public funding agency for nanotechnology. it accounted for 30% of public funding of nanotechnology research in the european union last year. significant funding increases are expected over the duration of the seventh framework programme. the commission has proposed expanding funding for nanotechnology, with a new emphasis on developing infrastructures and projects assessing the risk of nanotechnology for humans and the environment. that is a key area, because, as well as the benefits, we must also recognise the potential risks. these must be carefully assessed. some concerns have already been raised about new applications. the action plan addresses these too. special projects and publicity in many languages will provide information and communication. there are projects to engage the public – presenting both sides of the argument; brochures explaining how nanotechnology works; and even dvds explaining the issues in simple terms for children. in addition, the european group on ethics in science and new technologies is working on an opinion on the ethics of nanomedicine, which we expect to be delivered to president barroso soon. the commission is committed to ensuring a balanced approach. what is fundamental is to have a high level of public health, safety, environmental and consumer protection. to do that, in europe we need to identify the safety concerns, collect data for a health and environmental impact assessment of the product, and act at the earliest possible stage through adjustments, where necessary, of risk assessment procedures for nanotechnology. the commission is also looking at the european legislation applicable to nanotechnology. we are assessing how adequate and appropriate that legislation is to deal with the increasing use of nanotechnologies. we also need to consider potential regulatory issues. lastly, we are active in many international fora, addressing new issues and seeking to develop a code of good conduct. i am very happy to note that the european parliament, through the report of mr ransdorf, fully recognises the important role to be played by nanosciences and nanotechnologies and welcomes the commission’s action plan. i find it very positive that the report calls for increased public investment in related research and development, particularly in developing relevant infrastructures and nanomedicine. it is equally important that it stresses the importance of creating the right climate for innovation in europe as well as emphasising the importance of ‘speaking with one voice’ internationally in this highly promising research area. i am very happy to note that the report has enjoyed a very large measure of support from on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. nanoscience is concerned with phenomena in solids at the nano level, that is, at the 10- to 9-meter scale. based on this research, nanotechnology represents, as rarely as a high-priority area of technology, the most promising potential trend that will dramatically increase the likelihood of progress in many areas of our lives. this includes the automotive and aerospace industries, e.g. for the production of smooth and abrasion-resistant lacquers containing nanoparticles, health, e.g. for the production of pharmaceuticals or cosmetics, energy, for fuel cells and nanoporous hydrogen absorbers, as well as efficient solar batteries, itc techniques using optical and spin phenomena to further compress blue laser-readable information, biotechnology, including dna testing and bioinformatics systems. these examples can be extended to include sensor and structural materials such as nanocomposites and electron beam-surface activated fibres and fabrics. at the same time, unfortunately, there can be a permanent environmental contamination, a permanent air pollution, aerosol, which is difficult to monitor. there are two groups of nanotechnologies. group 1, 'top-down' technologies, including, inter alia, transition from macro to nano state, e.g. by grinding powders, expanding and activating their surfaces by increasing the potential. these technologies include, but are not limited to, the application of diamond protective coatings. group two, 'bottom-up' technologies allowing the shaping of the molecular level, e.g. for the production of highly integrated spinotronic devices. in this case, we have very few technologies available, unfortunately, that use tunnel microscopy or self-organizing phenomena. this group includes biological information systems. in conclusion, it should be noted that the scientific policy on nanoscience and nanotechnology should take into account the fact that, firstly, the development of 'top-down' technologies in the european union so far allows the establishment of at least a few, and even a dozen, technology platforms. secondly, bottom-up technologies require further intensive upstream research in the basic sciences. and thirdly, we must urgently develop a methodology to study the current pollution, i repeat, the current non-nanotechnology pollution, of the atmosphere with nanoparticles. it is more than just pm 2.5, which easily penetrates our bodies through cell membranes and whose catalytic action can be hazardous to health. who knows if the cancer epidemic is not linked to the elusive and perhaps increasing presence of persistent nanoaerosols in our environment from various sources.

mr. chairman, please! in may this year, we approved at second reading the regulation of the european parliament and of the council on nutrition and health claims made on foods, which means that from 1 january 2007 european law will require food manufacturers to put reliable information on the properties of the product on their packaging. in practice, this means that any health benefits of the goods must be established by independent laboratories. unfortunately, these regulations will only be ostensibly pro-consumer. the eu provision may eliminate products from small and medium-sized enterprises that cannot afford to pay for research by the standards of wealthy european companies. as a result, buyers will have less and less choice and less ability to make informed purchases, still not knowing what they are buying. the destructive mechanism of such competition can be curbed by licensing the right to award health-related labels and by standardising the remuneration of health-related products. it is also essential to give special support to small and mediumsized enterprises whose products are often of a much higher quality than those of the large companies entering our common market.

member of the commission. mr president, on behalf of my colleague peter mandelson, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and the committee on international trade on the report on economic and trade relations between the eu and mercosur with a view to the conclusion of an interregional association agreement. this report gives a very comprehensive picture of the current relations between the eu and mercosur in the economic as well as the political field, and the european commission shares most of the analysis presented in this report. the european commission very much concurs with the committee on international trade in its view that a conclusion of an ambitious and balanced association agreement between the eu and mercosur is a strategic objective. the commission remains firmly committed to concluding the agreement with mercosur as soon as it is technically and politically feasible. such an agreement would be the platform for promoting the relationship between the two regions and for promoting the common values and objectives that unite us. an eu-mercosur agreement would establish the first ever region-to-region association and the largest free-trade area in the world, covering almost 700 million people. as the inta report points out, such an association agreement would enable both regions to respond more effectively to the challenges of globalisation. it would enhance the competitiveness of our economies, increase growth and thereby contribute to economic and social cohesion. creating the world’s largest market place would give an enormous boost to job creation, economic reform and productivity levels. a free-trade agreement with mercosur is a very good example of how eu trade policy can contribute to the eu’s wider approach to economic reform and competitiveness. a region-to-region agreement with mercosur would also serve as an instrument to support an integration effort within mercosur and latin america. the accession of venezuela to mercosur this year implies an enlargement of the region and the european commission also hopes that the process of broadening and deepening regional integration will continue. we know from our own european experience that the reforms and adjustments necessary for integration are not easy. but we also know that the rewards make the effort worthwhile. an agreement would also create a more transparent and stable business environment for the eu and mercosur companies. this would contribute to attracting more investment flows. investment – and future investment – could possibly have the biggest impact on the shape of our future economic partnership with mercosur. although foreign direct investment to mercosur increased in 2004 and 2005, the relative share of the region in relation to global eu investments has been sliding ever since the 1990s. this is a source of concern, as investment means transfer of know-how, of industrialisation and jobs. this relative downward trend of the mercosur region in relation to the rest of the world, especially asia, is one of the challenges of the future agreement and, possibly, its main potential economic benefit. let me just say a few words on the timing. in the report by the international trade committee, you request the establishment of a negotiating calendar which would allow us to conclude the eu-mercosur negotiations as soon as possible. the european commission is fully committed to concluding these negotiations as soon as is technically and politically feasible, but we have always been of the opinion that substance prevails over timing. what we want to achieve is an ambitious, comprehensive and balanced agreement which goes beyond our wto commitments. as the inta report points out, there is a cost to not having an agreement. but there is also a long-term cost in missed opportunities from having a bad agreement. related to the issue of timing is the link between these biregional negotiations, the progress of the wto doha development agenda and the sequence of the two negotiations. in this respect, the european commission fully agrees with the analysis of the report by inta; both these processes can realise substantial synergies. they are not mutually exclusive; they are complementary. to conclude, let me convey to you the following message, which i am sure that you share with me: for strategic and political reasons, the european commission remains committed to negotiating and concluding an ambitious and balanced agreement with mercosur. trade is an important element of this agreement but not the only one. beyond the trade negotiations, we should not lose sight of the strategic, political and economic rationale of this agreement. let us not forget the strategic dimension of a future association agreement, which is to promote a relationship between regional blocs which enhances peace, stability, prosperity, social progress and democracy.

companies. the additional duties are to be set at 0%, 12,6% or 32,4%, as the case may be. thirdly, support mechanisms for producer groups should be introduced to give producers a stronger incentive to form groups, for example by doubling the aid rate for established and provisionally recognised groups. fourthly, other instruments should be introduced, such as special safeguard clauses (ssg), entry subsidies. a similar solution is proposed for the reform of the banana market, where the rules for calculating production subsidies expressed in tonnes are changed to area subsidies. in order to increase the competitiveness of the sector, these payments could be linked to the condition of compulsory participation in producer groups or organisations as well as to the compulsory sale of products under contract. the resolution also contains a number of other interesting actions and proposals. the soft fruit growers have lost three years and the current pace of reform of the market vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. i would like to deal briefly with the question of pfoa and then make a very basic remark. the last word on the pfoa matter has not been said. it has not been possible to include the prohibition of these substances in this directive because we do not have a sufficient risk assessment and we do not have an impact assessment. but there is an international risk assessment at the oecd level. we will of course look at the results carefully and make appropriate proposals if necessary. i live in the same german land as mr liese and have followed the case he has described with great interest. all i can say today is this: the german authorities' investigations are not yet complete, but i have the strong impression that we are dealing with a case of environmental crime. toxic substances have been released into the environment in violation of existing legislation. whether this could have been prevented by these directives is another matter. but the risks mr liese has described have been explicitly confirmed in this way once again, and that is why i thought it important that he referred to this case. in a modern industrial society, it will always be inevitable to live with certain risks. the question of which risks we consider acceptable and which we do not is one we have to decide again and again. there are a number of assessment criteria that can help us to do this. i would like to mention one that i do not accept. i do not accept the argument that we have to accept the risk of highly toxic substances in our environment because there has been investment. i do not accept the argument that we should accept such substances because they are profitable. i do not even accept the argument - even if i am not making friends now - that we should use these substances because they will keep jobs. i think that this juxtaposition of industrial jobs and the use of toxic substances which can be substituted is completely inappropriate. in such a situation, the only choice is to protect people and the environment unconditionally from risks that are not inevitable. that is the line which underlies my policy on all these matters. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental legislation is properly applied.

the next item is the report by mrs cristian muscardini, on behalf of the committee on foreign trade, on the annual report from the commission to the european parliament on the anti-dumping, anti-subsidy and safeguard measures taken by third countries against the community (2004) (2006/2136 (ini)) (a6-0243/2006)
mr. chairman, please! i would like to thank the rapporteur for her very comprehensive report on the protectionist measures used by third countries against the european union. the analysis of the rapporteur's report and the commission's report unfortunately confirms that european trade policy, especially in agriculture, is too strongly oriented towards protecting producers, and consumers pay the highest price. import quotas, anti-dumping duties and administrative barriers on agricultural products cost every european family about $1,500 a year. it seems clear, however, that sometimes, but in very limited and narrowly defined cases, the use of protective measures may be permissible. however, decisions to introduce them must be defined, planned and widely disseminated in advance, so that traders can plan their orders or deliveries in advance. the commission considers that the measures provided for in this decision are in line with the principles of the union state aid rules and are in accordance with the principle of proportionality, it is therefore very important that trade policy is predictable and stable. preferential rates must be understandable and easy to apply, and their introduction should be discussed extensively with all trading partners beforehand, so that every trader can be well informed and confident about the future of his orders. my final point concerns trade with developing countries, the wto and the european union. developing countries should make the most of the opportunities offered by their participation in the world trade organization. they should be treated as equal partners, and therefore the protection of the interests of large companies, mainly from the european union, but also from the usa, by the industrialized countries should not take place.
member of the commission. mr president, i have never been a unilateral disarmer at any stage in my political career, in any context. i have always been a multilateralist, whether it be in respect of disarmament or the putting in place of international rules to create institutions of global governance or in the design of processes to create agreements or to solve disputes in the world. i bring subject of trade is my belief in free trade. i say it is moral because i believe that free trade is the best way to drive economic growth, to lever up living standards, to create opportunities for that in respect not only of market access but also of trade rules and their strengthening, and that is what the commission remains dedicated to achieving.

member of the commission. the aim of the posting of workers directive is to reconcile the right of undertakings to provide crossborder services with the rights of posted workers. this is to be done while respecting the fundamental freedoms of movement of workers and services and the social legislation designed to protect workers. ten years after the adoption of this directive, difficulties in its implementation persist. first, workers and employers are not sufficiently informed about their rights and obligations. another problem is the lack of administrative cooperation between the authorities of the country of origin and the host country. in this respect, we can even speak of a certain mutual distrust. finally, the control measures applied by some member states raise concerns about protectionism. host country authorities have been granted some control rights, but even this has its limitations. these checks must be carried out on a proportionate scale, without discrimination, in order to guarantee the free movement of services within the internal market. in order to clarify this point, the commission considered it appropriate to adopt guidelines on 4 april. national authorities must provide posted workers and service providers with effective means of obtaining information on the working conditions applicable in the host country. they must also cooperate loyally with one another. in this respect, the commission considers it necessary to remind member states of their obligations and to call on them to put in place more effective means. i am aware that the debate in parliament on posting has been difficult and that there have been very different views. this, in my view, demonstrates how difficult it is to strike a balance between ensuring the protection of workers on the one hand and the free movement of services on the other. i am pleased to find that the report on which parliament voted shares many of the points made by the commission in its communication of 4 april. there are, however, a number of points to which i would like to pay particular attention and to which i would like to make a clear statement. i cannot agree with the view that the commission is seeking, through its opinion, to include the deleted articles 24 and 25 of the original draft services directive, because that is not the case and the commission is interpreting the law in question in its communication and not introducing a new law, since the commission's communication does not even formally provide for such a possibility, that is a matter of the legislative process. therefore, this claim does not correspond to reality in the interpretation used by the commission. i would stress again that the commission's communication does not establish a new law on which to base those articles, but interprets existing law, including important judgments of the luxembourg court. the court of justice judgments referred to in the commission notice prohibit national authorities from requiring service providers established in another member state to have a branch or representative established in their territory. the court has held that the host member state, in whose territory the foreign service provider provides services, may, subject to compliance with the principle of solidarity, require that documents directly relating to the work in question, in particular the work records or documents relating to health, safety and security at work, be made available at the workplace. in its interpretation, the commission in no way limits the member states' ability to carry out effective checks, none of the above formulations is directed towards that objective and i must state that the commission has made a very careful effort in its interpretation to identify and capture the substance and spirit of individual judgments. the commission attaches particular importance to the proper implementation of the directive and will increase its monitoring of this implementation. it has already started work on a report to assess the situation one year after the publication of the guidelines. to this end, the commission sent a questionnaire to the national authorities and the social partners. it also set up a website devoted to the legal and practical issues of posting. it has recently published a form on this site, through which any european citizen can make suggestions and comments. in addition, a group of national experts working under the auspices of the commission has developed a code of good practice laying down certain rules on administrative cooperation and a standard form to facilitate the exchange of information between contact points. the commission naturally takes account of all the views of parliament and considers the report under consideration to be an important document.
