mr. chairman, please! while welcoming the european central bank's performance in 2005, i would like to stress that the group of european socialists fully respects and supports the independence of the central bank. we believe that this independence is a necessary condition for the conduct of a sound monetary policy in the economic and monetary union and a guarantee of the value of our common currency. i would now like to draw attention to three issues which have been the subject of debate in our parliament for a long time. first, we are not clear about the relative weight of the two pillars of monetary policy that the ecb uses, namely the money supply and other information about future inflation. consequently, it is not known whether and to what extent the money supply is a decisive factor in the ecb's interest rate policy. the announcement of clear rules on this issue would make monetary policy more transparent and effective. second, there is an urgent need for a clear interpretation of the ecb's mandate as set out in article 105 (1) of the treaty. in particular, the ecb should announce how and by what means it intends to fulfil its treaty obligation to support the economic policies of the european union while maintaining price stability. i would point out that the treaty clearly distinguishes between the two objectives and that they cannot be treated as substitutes. a clear ecb position on this issue would avoid any confusion as to whether the ecb is responsible for pursuing objectives other than price stability. third, the ecb is wrong in its interpretation of the inflation criterion used to assess the degree of readiness of new member states to join the euro area. the treaty clearly states that the reference point is the average inflation rate in the three countries with the best price stability performance. the treaty doesn't say anything about the lowest price. the ecb has defined price stability as an inflation rate below but close to 2%, but in assessing the degree of preparedness of the candidate countries the ecb uses a different definition, namely the average of the three countries with the lowest inflation rates. since there cannot be two different definitions of the same treaty term, i ask the ecb to clarify this issue.
the european central bank mr president, perhaps i can say something, since a number of questions have been raised. i would first like to thank the members of parliament. i was very impressed by the precision of the remarks, observations and recommendations made to us. on the subject of independence, i would like to say, on behalf of all the members of the executive board and the governing council of the european central bank, how important it is to hear so many members of parliament say that the independence of the central bank is an absolutely major issue. i must confess that we could not have given the european economy the monetary and financial environment it deserves without the credibility that this principle of independence gives us, which is recognized by your parliament, by the whole world and by all market participants everywhere in the world. this is in the treaty, it is recognised and it is a fundamental asset of europe. i would like to thank once again all the members who have spoken so clearly on this point. let me now deal with some of the other points raised, which are certainly important in the eyes of a number of members of parliament. i have to say that the question of the appointment of the members of the executive board is one that should be addressed to the executive branches, particularly the council, because they are responsible for such matters. we are appointed in accordance with the treaty provisions and, as you know, not only does the parliament give its assessment of the quality of the various persons concerned, but so do we in the governing council. i know that parliament would like to have not only an advisory role but also responsibility for the decision itself. i respect that sentiment. i realise that the ecb has to let parliament and the council discuss the matter, provided that full independence and absence of politicization are totally assured, for, clearly, if the institution were to suffer from politicization, it would not be able to deliver what it has to deliver, namely, price stability, something which also depends on it enjoying sound credibility, so that inflation expectations can be firmly anchored. as regards the various remarks on the dialogue between parliament and the ecb, in my opinion this dialogue has improved in terms of both frequency and interaction and i will take good note of all the remarks made here, including those concerning the governance of our possible target2 securities system. on that issue, which is dear to your heart, mr radwan, and to that of other members of parliament, i would say that our aspiration - and it is really a work in progress - was to maximise the benefits of european integration following the successful introduction of the euro, since it is clear that the availability of a single settlement engine for securities denominated in euros would undoubtedly represent progress. the second objective would be to maximise settlement efficiency and that would probably require cash and securities to be settled on the same it platform, according to what is known technically as an 'integrated model'. the third issue, which is important from our own perspective, is how to maximize the central bank's control over the bank accounts opened in our own book. we take a very strong line on this, believing that solutions which avoid forcing central banks to outsource the management of their accounts would not be good ones. these are the three main reasons why we are working on this matter, through a dialogue with the market, which is very important, and, of course, with parliament. a number of other points have been mentioned. i will not return to the matter of hedge funds raised by mrs van den burg, in particular. as to the question of whether or not we are sufficiently transparent and open in terms of communication, i reiterate that we do not take decisions alone behind closed doors. the commissioner and the president of the eurogroup, jean-claude juncker, are invited to all meetings of the governing council. they are also invited every fortnight to our discussions and deliberations, so that they can be as close as possible to the decisions taken. i myself have the privilege of appearing before the eurogroup every month. so there are three opportunities each month to exchange views and gain as full as possible an understanding of how the decision-making process really works. it seems to me that, from that standpoint, we have the most highly organized system of contacts anywhere in the world. it is not new; it was the tradition of the bundesbank, the banque de france and a number of central banks. let us not underestimate its significance. some of the remarks made fail to take this into account. as regards the transparency of our concept of monetary policy, we are in a position where we say that our primary goal is price stability, because that is what the treaty stipulates. we give an arithmetical definition of price stability as inflation rates of below and close to 2%. everyone is aware of this. we have a two-pillar strategy that is very clear. in that respect, we are much more transparent and precise. we provide a greater yardstick with which to measure our performance than other sister central banks do. i do not want to address myself to any of them in particular, but across the atlantic there is a sister central bank which, for very good reasons of its own, has a different approach to the definition of price stability, with regard to the clarity of that goal. from that standpoint we are very transparent. the entire world knows that we are transparent and it is one of the reasons why inflation expectations are anchored in line with our definition of price stability, which is a fundamental result. mr president, i would like to say a few words to a few members. the fact that we are credible and that our inflation expectations are in line with our definition of price stability provides a particularly favourable financial environment for the european economy. i would ask those members who have criticised our monetary policy as being too orthodox to simply recall what the medium and longterm market interest rates were in their countries before the introduction of the euro. in reality, inflation expectations were based on inflation that was much higher than what we can guarantee to europeans today. it is worth noting that low inflation is a fundamental element for the poorest among us, preserving their purchasing power. i have noticed that many members have asked us to be very vigilant in this respect. i am therefore deeply convinced that there is a very simple relationship between our primary objective as set out in the treaty and article 105. the first objective is a necessary but not sufficient condition for us to move in the direction that everyone in this house wants, namely, of course, growth and employment. price stability is a necessary condition for sustainable growth and for the creation of sustainable jobs. if i have time i shall make two or three other remarks. regarding the 500 euro note, i do not agree at all with the remark that was made suggesting that we would actively assist money laundering. as you know, large denomination notes were a strong tradition in many of the countries forming part of the euro area and we decided not to change the various traditions drastically. so the note is used in some countries, but not in others. it remains an option and we decided not to eliminate that option for those countries and economies that were used to it. i believe i have covered all the other questions that were raised. however, mr whittaker mentioned the one-size-fits-all angle. europe is a vast continental economy and, from 1 january next year when slovenia joins, the eurozone will have 315 million citizens. this compares with 300 million in the united states and thus represents an economy of the same order of magnitude. when you measure the dispersion, the standard deviation of growth and of inflation at the level of various states of various different sizes, you will see that it is roughly the same for both economies. this is not widely known, but is worth pointing out, since it appears to be a characteristic of a vast continental economy. this does not mean that we have to cater for persistent differences, and it is one of the things that we have discussed, particularly in the eurogroup. we need to reflect on this question, but again, it would probably be wrong to forget that an element of dispersion is always associated with the size of the economy concerned. mr president, i think i have covered most of the questions that were asked, but of course i remain at mr. chairman, please! i voted in favour of the amended draft services directive. in other words, i was against her being rejected. as i am generally optimistic, i believe that it will contribute to reducing bureaucracy, to economic growth and to the creation of new jobs. but let's be honest, the original version of the directive, proposed by the european commission three years ago, was much better and could have done a better job of meeting the lisbon objectives. the current directive is seriously watered down and it is difficult to speak of a great success. some of the old member states of the union seem to fear the freedom to provide services and to compete with the new countries, explaining this by social dumping. it is difficult to understand, because i think we all want europe to be dynamic and competitive.
in writing. the only advantage of the compromise on the services directive is that its adoption will not undermine the principles of the functioning of the services market. that's the only reason we can support this compromise in today's vote. the final outcome of the operation of this directive will be determined by the european court of justice, which will no doubt rule on disputes based on contradictory provisions of the directive on many occasions. on the one hand, we have the declared freedom to provide services. on the other hand, we have the exclusion of the operation of this directive in the field of undefined public and social services and temporary agency work, the exclusion of the impact of the directive on the form of labour law and collective agreements and the elimination of restrictions on the work of posted workers. this means that no significant barriers to the provision of services in the eu will be removed with the adoption of the services directive. this is a 100% compromise at the expense of the new member states, which have a competitive advantage on the union market in the services sector. all the social motives for introducing these exceptions and limitations do not fulfil their declared social role. they are only an alibi for the economic chauvinism of the trade unions and other interest groups in the countries of the old european union. the debate on this project so far is the biggest display of european hypocrisy in this term. the european parliament, and the whole of the union behind it, pretends to introduce the rules of the common market in services. we are not only deceiving ourselves, but our citizens.
mr. chairman, please! the european parliament resolution supports the northern dimension policy and defines the north sea region as a priority area. since the enlargement in 2004, the baltic sea has become almost an internal sea, the 'mare nostrum' of the european union. this region can become the most dynamic economic region in the union, demonstrating the development of a european economy based on the latest technologies, modern and competitive on a global scale. the need to protect the baltic sea ecosystem, which is highly vulnerable due to its shallow, slow water change and high pollution, should therefore be emphasised. particular attention should be paid to fostering innovation in research and to addressing cultural and civil society issues. the baltic sea, which links the european union, russia, norway and iceland, should become an example of an area of peace and security. i would particularly like to highlight the joint analysis by the european union and russia of the possibilities of transforming the kaliningrad region into a pilot region with better access to the internal market. cooperation in the baltic sea region can show the future of this part of our continent, cooperation with russia and other countries.
mr. chairman, please! i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the preparation of a good report on the future of the baltic sea. however, when we talk about the specific features of a region, we cannot forget the important factors that shape its character. one is the historical legacy of the chemical weapons stockpiles from world war ii still lying at the bottom of the baltic. this is coupled with the issue of a fragile ecosystem, which is further threatened by heavy shipping and planned investments, such as the construction of the northern gas pipeline, which could lead to an ecological disaster. when undertaking such projects, it is necessary to carefully examine their potential impact on the environment, consult with stakeholders and possibly abandon the planned works if it is found that they may have a negative impact on the baltic ecosystem. environmental issues and the interests of the countries of the region must also be taken into account in the creation of the planned maritime highway. equal access to its benefits should be ensured for baltic ports. it is important to ensure close cooperation between member states in the construction of energy networks and to ensure solidarity between the union and russia. poland is currently blocking the deal with russia until it opens up to our meat and agricultural products. the union responded by saying that the west would not be cold for polish sausage. there was a time when people said, "we don't want to die for gdansk", and we know how that ended. mr. chairman, please! the baltic sea, which is now almost an internal sea of the union, is of priority importance both for the region's economy and for the european union as a whole. unfortunately, the baltic sea is the most polluted sea in the world. it therefore needs help, in other words a common strategy and consistent cooperation between the eu and russia to implement it. it is therefore fitting that agreement on a new political declaration on the northern dimension and a framework strategic document will be the subject of discussions at the eu-russia summit in helsinki on 24 november. when we take up the problem of the baltic sea, we must remember that its basin is home to some 85 million people and that it contains a wealth of natural resources, including many endangered species. the sea has fed millions of people for centuries, supporting not only families of fishermen but also other trades. the people of the sea have also created their own culture, which we should protect as carefully as the natural environment, landscape and material values. we therefore look with concern to the planned northern gas pipeline and the associated dangers of chemical contamination and militarization. the baltic sea is a treasure that we have inherited from our ancestors, with the duty to pass it and its values on to future generations.
mr. chairman, please! the northern dimension of the union's external policy is not only a priority for the finnish presidency, it is also a very important direction for polish foreign policy and the foreign policy of the seven baltic member states of the european union. the baltic has been a zone of peaceful cooperation with russia for several years. to keep this up, it is necessary to eliminate the threats that are on the horizon today. i am thinking primarily of the first: the growing dependence of the countries of the region on russian energy supplies and the second, the package of unresolved problems in the kaliningrad region. these challenges are beyond the capacity of each country individually, and beyond the capacity of all eight of us, and it is therefore essential that they become a priority for the european union as a whole. today, as much as 24% of our gas supply comes from russia. in the future, this percentage will increase. the possibility of a gas cartel being set up by the russian side, mentioned by charles tannock a moment ago, is of additional concern. investments such as the baltic gas pipeline increase the eu's dependence on its eastern neighbour. moreover, they create dangerous political tensions between partners within the union itself. the kaliningrad region is a ticking time bomb. worrying is not only the degree of militarization, but also the social situation in kaliningrad: the high percentage of residents infected with aids, the devastation of the environment and the spread of organized crime. so without a common interest on the part of the whole union in these problems, i emphasize, there will be no common policy either on energy or on kaliningrad. and without a common policy, we all lose, we all fail.
mr. chairman, please! i would like to expand on the kaliningrad theme, because kaliningrad is a big challenge. we all hoped that kaliningrad would be to russia what hong kong was to china, but there are concerns that it could be what puerto rico has become to the united states. apart from the dangers mentioned by the previous speaker, mr klich, i would like to draw attention to another unresolved problem, namely that 15 years after the fall of the berlin wall and the end of the cold war, there is a huge amount of armaments in kaliningrad that we simply do not know what they are doing there. the numbers are available because russia, as a signatory to the treaty on conventional arms control, is required to make those numbers public. there are more tanks in kaliningrad than in the british and french armies combined. what are they for, anyway? it's been 15 years, i repeat, since the end of the cold war. the whole package of problems must therefore be solved together with russia, because the future of the baltic sea region will depend to a large extent on the future of the kaliningrad region. and it's probably the most dynamic region today, and its chances of further dynamism are enormous.
mr. chairman, please! i believe that today the baltic sea region will increasingly unite rather than divide the countries of the region by pursuing and strengthening economic interests while respecting their political rights and preserving their environmental heritage. but this will not be possible if the concentration of economic interests is based solely on the pursuit of particular interests, without respect for the principles of good neighbourly cooperation, solidarity and shared responsibility, as is the case, for example, with the construction of the northern gas pipeline, which is mentioned here repeatedly, an investment carried out without the agreement of the baltic sea partners. we must answer the question today: what is the purpose of deepening cooperation among the eight baltic countries, what are the priorities? on the one hand, we are advocating the need to protect the baltic sea ecosystem, but on the other hand we are afraid to have an open and honest debate about the ecological aspects of the construction of the pipeline. i remind you that last year 60 members of this house signed a petition calling for a debate on the environmental aspects of the pipeline. this debate never took place, it was never put on the agenda by the chairmen. i would also like to inform the representatives of the council and the commission that russia is blocking freedom of navigation in the baltic sea by not allowing vessels to pass through the strait between the gulf of vistula and kaliningrad. the polish port of elbląg, which had just been renovated with european money, was thus dying, and it was losing its access to the open sea. the mountain is occupied by russia's unilateral interests, which has its military base over the strait. the baltic strategy recognises these threats, and i thank alexander stubb for his report, he can count on our support for the objectives he wants to pursue, and i also extend my thanks to all the members of the baltic intergroup and its chairman, christopher beazley, for his commitment.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i warmly congratulate the report on european security policy. this is a very good report which, in my view, does not require any further amendments, in particular no amendments which would deprive the european union of any significance in the world military game. the union, if it is to play a growing role in the world, must demonstrate the capacity for an effective military presence not only at its borders but also in other regions of the world. the creation of a defense agency and the harmonization of weapons will not help. we also need to convince the european public to spend more on defence, proportionate to our aspirations. europe has proven that it does not abuse military force, so the pacifist concerns raised in this case are unfounded. on the contrary, we have to fear for our political and military capacity to take responsibility for world security. the construction of a european security policy cannot be geared to duplicating nato, our main and proven instrument of defence policy. our strategic autonomy should not be used to create a dysfunction in political and technical cooperation with the forces of the north atlantic alliance. on the contrary, the western world, which extends far beyond the union's borders, has the right to expect us to make a substantial contribution to cooperation and synergy in our joint activities. it has been balanced in the report and we will therefore be happy to support it in the vote tomorrow.
madam president! today's debate on the implementation of the european security strategy is one of the most important discussions on the future of the union. it is part of the partial acceptance of some of the solutions contained in the dead constitutional treaty. the proposal to appoint a european minister for foreign affairs and defence is dangerous to the interests of many member states. the example of european solidarity in the energy sector was given by germany in its agreement with russia. it is most characteristic and warning. it is understandable that the union should have an instrument of military influence on its immediate environment. however, the attempt to take responsibility for global security in the military dimension is an attempt to replace nato, or more precisely to weaken the influence of the united states in europe and the world. there can be no competition between nato and the european union in the field of security and defence policy. it should be stressed that nato is of far greater importance and potential than the separate armed forces of the union. of course, there are non-nato members of the union, and we need to find a formula for them to engage in european security issues. such cooperation shall take place in the field of cooperation between the national armies of the member states of the union. we don't need to create new commands, we just need to separate the components of the national armed forces to cooperate in specific actions. the need is to create a coherent european intelligence, crisis response and economic threat monitoring system. it is the concern of the nation states and the union to check how each member is prepared for terrorist attacks, whether they have an appropriate system of organizing territorial defence forces. the union's concern should be security in its immediate surroundings, not global influence and involvement in local conflicts in the world.
madam president! the solana strategy of 2003 is a great document. it describes the threats and challenges we face and sets out clearly this specifically european approach to responding, which has become the hallmark of european security and defence policy. in this sense, it does not appear that the document needs to be updated. after all, nato has been using the same strategic concept since april 1999. and that is the only aspect of karl von wogau's proposal that i disagree with. the value of his report lies in something else, in the perspective he has created for epbo. this report is the result of a fair assessment of the current civil-military capabilities of the european union, when karl von wogau says that, "the union currently has only limited capabilities to conduct civil and military operations". karl von wogau draws the right conclusions from this assessment, firstly by calling for intensive cooperation between the european union and nato, and secondly by calling for the union's potential to be concentrated in our immediate geographical neighbourhood. the rapporteur is aware of the source of these limitations when he points to the lack of strategic air and sea transport, interoperable telecommunications systems, and intelligence capabilities, especially satellite capabilities. well, this is not a new observation, because these gaps have been with us at least since the first capabilities commitment conference in 2000. however, the greatest asset of this report, in my view, is the long-term perspective that karl von wogau has created for the epbo. it goes beyond the operational objective, that is to say beyond 2010, and beyond the provisions of the constitutional treaty. the prospect is to create a security and defence union. this is the perspective we must not lose sight of, because it is and should be the compass for the next steps in the development of the epbo.
madam president! i would like to start by quoting a eurobarometer survey which shows that 70% of the european union's citizens support european security and defence policy. the citizens of the union seem to have a better grasp of the challenges of our time than the council representatives, absent from the plenary in strasbourg this evening. the european security strategy should focus on the key objectives in the development of the common security and defence policy of the european union. first of all, it is necessary to demand the integration of the new generation of satellite reconnaissance systems into the european system and the provision of the data thus collected for military, police and disaster management purposes via the satellite centre in torrejón. intelligence remains one of the most important areas of this strategy. secondly, the rapid reaction groups currently being set up must be equipped with the same or at least compatible intelligence and telecommunications equipment as nato.
madam president! the achievement of the objectives set out in the security strategy depends to a large extent on the union's ability to implement that document, which in turn will give the union credibility as a serious security policy actor; an actor that acts decisively in a crisis situation. in the face of current challenges to european foreign policy, such as conflicts in the middle east, military missions involving troops from eu member states, and the rise of new leaders such as china and india, it is necessary to strengthen the common foreign and security policy. in order to make the cfsp more effective and efficient, today we need milestones and answers to the fundamental questions raised by the unadopted constitutional treaty. it also requires individuals and institutions to steer the policy, such as the eu's foreign minister, more funding, better analysis of key issues and coordination of eu member states' policies. it is important to build up own capacities for humanitarian operations, peacekeeping and peace-building, and crisis management. an effective multilateral system and a stable neighbourhood are the means of ensuring the security of the member states of the union. the implementation of the strategy depends to a large extent on the will of the member states and the proper performance of the obligations imposed on them. the adoption of a legislative framework, a timetable for further action and a commitment to external relations are not sufficient to create an effective system for preventing and combating threats.

"women represent half of the potential of human talents and skills and their under-representation at decision-making level remains to the detriment of society as a whole". it's a quote from the athens ministerial declaration of 14 years ago. despite many similar political declarations, specific action programmes and legislation, the phenomenon of gender discrimination has not disappeared. of the nearly 44,000 parliamentarians in the world, only 16% are women, and of the 191 countries that are currently members of the united nations, only seven have a woman as their highest-ranking head of state, and eight have a woman as their head of government. the absence of women in the political process and decision-making is sometimes linked to difficulties in reconciling social, family and professional life, and is often also the result of discrimination in employment and vocational training. the european union should be an example to the world in promoting equality and democracy, but even here in the european parliament, women make up only 30% of meps. there are countries like cyprus and malta that have no women representatives. member states and political parties across europe should aim for a so-called 'balance gap': between 40 and 60% representation of each gender on the electoral roll. then the representation of the public would be really adequate. i congratulate mrs gomes on a great report which will hopefully contribute to a change in the position of women in political life.
mr. chairman, please! the fight against trafficking in human beings is the great challenge of the 21st century. in the fight for human dignity and to curb this practice, international and national organizations have signed a number of declarations, conventions, directives and are taking a number of actions. the rapporteur notes that these measures reduce trafficking in human beings in a broad sense, but do not eliminate its causes. the causes include: unemployment, hunger, the impoverishment of large social groups, high indirect labour costs, competition, the desire to maximise profit, which often stimulates undeclared work, the tolerance of slave labour by local communities (for example, the case of the italian city of foggia) and sexual violence, ethnic conflicts and wars. the report can serve as a basis for the development of programmes for further economic, legal and political, educational, information and institutional action, the implementation of which will reduce trafficking in human beings, which is contrary to the principles of democracy and human dignity.
mr. chairman, please! i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur on her report, which deals with a very important subject of socio-political importance. human trafficking is a global problem and a modern form of slavery that violates basic human rights. the trafficking of women and children is a particularly tragic element of this practice. i'd like to focus on the economic aspects of this phenomenon. it should be noted that trafficking in human beings involves both supply and demand drivers. on the one hand, the lack of a sustainable economic and social future, high unemployment and the prospect of ever-increasing poverty in some developing countries compared to the level of economic and social development in europe, contribute to a situation in which it is easy for criminal organisations to profit from trafficking in human beings. on the other hand, it should be taken into account that the demand for cheap, unregistered and submissive workers in the european union contributes to trafficking in human beings, as the use of such labour can reduce costs. however, this is done at the expense of human dignity and damages employment standards, health and safety measures, fair wages and local and national income through non-payment of taxes and insurance premiums. trafficking in human beings is the fastest growing criminal activity compared to other forms of organised crime in the european union, and measures taken to date to curb trafficking in human beings have not yet produced the desired results. the difficulties in combating this practice are obvious, but the european union's commitment must be firm. the report presented, which proposes an integrated approach and a proposal for an action plan, should therefore be welcomed.

in the meantime. the petitioners stressed that it has been 30 years since famagusta was conquered by the turkish army and its part, called varosha, was closed. in presenting their concerns and petition to our committee, the petitioners pointed out that varosha, which has become a completely extinct city, is causing deep divisions among the displaced residents and also among their descendants, hindering the overall economic revival of the city and not contributing to building trust between the cypriot communities. specifically, the petitioners propose the return of varosha to its original inhabitants in accordance with the regulations to be adopted by the international community, including, above all, the european union. the petitioners declared their support for the efforts to help the turkish cypriots, who are legally and sociologically an integral part of cyprus. they also expressed concern at the regulations in place for the benefit of the turkish cypriot community, regarding isolation and independence from the general deliberate strategy to reunify cyprus. the petitioners pointed out that although this is contained in the explanatory memorandum attached to the draft council regulation establishing a financial support instrument for the economic development of the turkish cypriot community, the package is intended to facilitate the reunification of cyprus by supporting economic and social development, with a particular focus on the economic integration of the islands. the petitioners, for their part, also and above all propose facilitating the promotion of trade and tourism, which can improve the welfare of the community and lead to an improvement in the financial situation, and the exploitation of the port of famagusta to its full potential, and consequently the regeneration of the entire surrounding area. the petitioners also proposed that part of the eu funds allocated to support turkish cypriot communities be allocated to a special fund managed by a non-governmental organisation with equal participation of both communities, under the patronage of the european union and the supervision of the european commission. and that this money be used for the renovation, operation and further modernization of the port of famagusta. the committee on petitions, on behalf of the petitioners, asked the european commission to indicate what instruments the european commission intends to use to ensure that the petitioners' case is resolved. the general affairs council of 27 february 2006 decided to call on the commission to make further efforts in the area of direct trade for the benefit of the turkish cypriot community on the basis of the negotiations which took place during the luxembourg presidency, when the issues of the varosha closed area and the port were raised alongside those relating to free trade. and then it was said that this area of famagusta, or varosha, is not used today. this situation is extremely painful for the displaced residents and their descendants, hinders the economic regeneration of the city and does not contribute to building trust between cypriot communities. so what does the commission intend to do in the light of this decision so that the famagusta exclusion zone is returned to its rightful residents? mr president, we have debated many times in this chamber the on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing the community customs code is the text which has made a thorough modernisation of the existing customs code of 1992. modernisation is necessary because of the radical changes that have taken place in the sphere of international trade. the regulation therefore aims to simplify customs legislation and procedures both from the point of view of economic operators and the customs administration, in order to reduce the cost of customs clearance and to meet the commercial challenges in the areas of safety and security, anti-counterfeiting, money laundering, health and environmental protection. the new community customs code has not only simplified certain procedures but has also made fundamental changes to customs law in certain respects. this document is inseparably linked to the proposal for the computerisation of customs procedures. the decision of the parliament and of the council on the electronic environment for customs and trade envisages the establishment and use of secure, interoperable and accessible electronic customs systems, which should simplify and improve supply chain logistics and customs processes. the third proposal establishing a community customs action programme customs 2013 enhances cooperation between customs administrations and their staff. operates trans-european information networks which enable customs control obligations to be fulfilled in the internal market and taxation of goods and services to be maintained in accordance with national and community tax legislation within the internal market. the programme plays a significant role in the smooth functioning of the internal market and the management of the external borders of the european union, and contributes to the achievement of the commission's objectives for 2005-2009 and the lisbon strategy.
mr. chairman, please! the customs system of the european union should fulfil two main tasks. first, to protect the community's economic and financial interests; second, to facilitate legitimate trade and to speed up and simplify customs procedures. unfortunately, despite the existence of the customs 2007 programme and the allocation of nearly eur 150 million for this purpose, these tasks are not fully implemented. suffice it to mention the negative impact on the community market of large-scale smuggling of alcohol, tobacco products and, more recently, liquid fuels. not only is the scale of this smuggling disrupting the internal market, but hundreds of millions of euros in customs duties are not coming into the union budget. this is also the case for food products. it is on this market that products are very often offered at prices well below their cost of production, which is a clear indication of circumvention. this has recently been the case in the poultry market in poland and for the last two years it has been the case with frozen strawberries imported from china. thus, the second objective of the customs system, which is to facilitate trade, is not fulfilled. this is particularly evident on the eu's eastern border with russia, belarus and ukraine. long procedures, long queues, corruption discourage the export of goods from the eu. i would like to express the hope that the amount of eur 323 million for the implementation of the customs 2013 programme will allow for a significant improvement.

member of the commission. mr president, firstly i would like to say that i am grateful for the work done by the members of the committees concerned with this commission proposal to amend decision 90/424/eec on expenditure in the veterinary field. this year, the commission allocated approximately eur 210 million to assist member states in running eradication and monitoring programmes to counter animal diseases. this programme is a key element in our food safety strategy. as we all know, animal diseases are unpredictable – the unexpected can and does happen. in 2005-2006 even though we saw outbreaks of avian flu, blue tongue and classical swine fever in some member states, none of them was a major outbreak and we managed to keep them under control and not allow them to cause extensive damage. the commission has embarked on a wide-ranging review of community animal health policy. an extensive evaluation has recently been completed and the results were presented at a conference held in brussels last month. i was pleased to note that several honourable members attended, and indeed chaired, sessions. one of the primary areas of interest for discussion today and one which generated considerable interest was the possible introduction of an insurance or cost-sharing element to help fund disease eradication costs. however, these are longer-term measures which still need considerable discussion with the various stakeholders before we can determine how best to proceed. there are, however, a number of key changes which we can make now, in order to improve efficiency in how the commission and the member states manage funding in this area. the proposal before us today aims to make such changes, while allowing the necessary time for other longer-term issues to be dealt with in the ongoing policy review. the proposal contains three main elements. first, we propose to introduce the possibility of multiannual programming for the disease eradication programmes, but with a simplified procedure which will make it easier both for the member states and also for the commission. second, we propose to strengthen the legal basis for the traces programme, but also for communication. it is interesting to note that we currently have a legal base for communication activities in animal welfare but not for animal health, and this is going to be corrected in the proposal. third, we propose to limit the list of disease eradication programmes eligible for funding to those that correspond to clear priorities, but with a procedure under which this list could be amended when necessary in response to developments. the proposed changes would make important advances in strengthening and prioritising our food safety strategy. the proposal makes a number of improvements which will also increase efficiency and reduce bureaucracy, both for the commission and the member states. i am grateful for parliament’s support.
mr. chairman, please! i would like to express my support, also as a veterinarian, for mrs figueiredo's report, particularly as regards the requirement that contagious animal diseases such as bovine leucosis and aujeszky's disease should be included in the list of diseases eligible for community co-financing. i would remind you that the eradication of these diseases is now of particular importance in many member states of the union, not least because of intra-community trade. one of the conditions for the admission of a pig herd to trade is that it comes from a region or country free of aujeszky's disease. the same applies to bovine animals which must come from herds officially free of enzootic bovine leukemia. many new member states do not have sufficient financial resources to fully eradicate these diseases due to budgetary constraints. the amendment proposed by the european commission to the list of diseases, to remove bovine leucosis and aujeszky's disease, could result in a significant reduction or even suspension of the control programmes being implemented. it is also a matter of priority that any future changes to the updating of the list of diseases should be subject to the consent of the european parliament and the council.
member of the commission. mr president, i welcome the interest shown by the members in the proposal to modify what we call the veterinary fund. i appreciate that the overall principles of the proposal have been accepted by parliament. the suggestions made are good ones but many of those are already being applied. the idea, for example, to allow emergency expenditure in a crisis is indeed essential, to delay the final date for submitting an application for funding, we encourage member states to submit applications as early in the year as possible. nevertheless, we can accept a final date of 30 mr. chairman, please! the amendment of the common organisation of the market in bananas proposed by the european commission is in line with the philosophy of the 2003 reform of the common agricultural policy and with the commitments that the union has made in the negotiations at the world trade organisation level. however, it is worth analysing the impact of the reform on the level of banana production in the outermost regions of the union. there is a certain similarity between the banana reform and the forthcoming reform of the soft fruit market. the regional dimension of the banana sector is as important as the size of the soft fruit market. the scale of the threat to the stability of rural areas and the income levels of farmers and their families is similar. both crops are extremely labor intensive. furthermore, it must be noted that the soft fruit market is more exposed to the illicit activities of third countries than the banana market. in the case of soft fruit, we have only temporary safeguard and anti-dumping procedures. we have an effective single tariff system for bananas. since some of the support instruments proposed for the banana market would solve the problem of the soft fruit market, the european commission should consider implementing them on this market. in particular, the introduction of an area payment scheme for soft fruit for processing. hopefully, the proposed regulations will have a positive impact on the situation of banana growers. we do, however, expect to see the real costs of this reform.

mr. chairman, please! i should like to begin by saying that i think all three reports should be supported and i thank the rapporteurs for their work. but first of all, i want to congratulate commissioner piebalgs. after two and a half years in office, we're talking about energy in a very different way than we did before. firstly, it has become clear today that our difficulties in europe are due to the threat to oil and gas supplies, and therefore the initiatives of the commissioner, the european commission and the european council to engage in an intensive dialogue with our partners, the suppliers of oil and gas, are worth supporting. we need a common foreign policy on energy supplies. the routes of energy supply are also important, not just the suppliers themselves. this is incredibly important. secondly, if we are to counter the crisis in gas and oil supplies, we must rely on europe's own energy sources. over the past two and a half years, the european union has clearly made energy saving and renewable energy a priority. we have it in all the documents, including the documents on research and development of new technologies. biofuels are of particular importance here. the necessary legal regulations are still needed. thirdly, the union is continuing the euratom programme, the oldest community programme, which has brought europe a relatively safe and reliable source of atomic energy. we have to keep going. renewable energy alone will not do it, although i support the colleagues who say that renewable energy is necessary. fourth, after years of neglect, europe has finally remembered that almost all countries have their own source of energy - coal. but there can be no going back to the 19th or 20th century way of using coal. it requires completely new technologies to exploit it. i congratulate you, commissioner, and all my colleagues on the fact that we have decided to take such action within the framework of the european union.
member of the commission. mr president, after such a full and very rich debate it is very difficult and challenging to respond to the points that have been raised, because each of the three reports deserved a separate debate. i shall try to emphasise the common rather than the divisive issues. firstly, it is very important that parliament state clearly that there is a challenge to act now. actions to combat climate change should be taken now – there is no time left. security of supply and the competitiveness of the european economy are also urgent matters. we should all like to see affordable prices for our industries and citizens. we should also like to ensure that energy is produced and used in a sustainable way. i think we agree on what should be done to achieve that. we should provide for long-term perspectives for investment; we should provide for the full use of market forces; we should provide for diversification of energy sources and suppliers. we know that we should focus strongly on energy efficiency. we know that there is consensus for a focus on renewable energy, including heating and cooling. we know that we should focus on research and development. it is also important to realise that if we act alone, although it might be good for us, it will not be enough. in order to do this we need the eu’s economies of scale and scope. however, it is also clear that, to achieve that, we must have a common vision and present legislation based on debate that responds not only to this vision but also to the principles of better legislation. we need a general consensus in europe. we need one voice and to take joint action. for those reasons i really believe that, when the commission adopts the package on 10 january 2007, this will open the door, as mr langen said, to real action and real legislative proposals – good proposals not only in the legislative field but also in other areas. i should like to thank mrs morgan, mr langen and mr seppänen for their excellent reports and the whole parliament for this debate. unfortunately i have to finish on a sad note because last night i received the very sad news that my predecessor, mrs loyola de palacio, has died. i wish to pay tribute to her. we will really miss her, because she was devoted not only to her energy remit but also to europe. she had very strong and clear views, which were not always shared by everyone. we need spirits like hers. i really believe that the best tribute we can pay her would be by taking very ambitious action towards creating a european energy policy and not being discouraged by legal hurdles. in this way we will commemorate her in the best possible way. i would like to express my support for the report by mr w. langen on the strategy for biomass and biofuels. renewable energy sources, in the context of increasing dependence on the supply of fuels and energy from third countries and the requirements to meet stricter standards for emissions into the environment, are one of the most important elements of energy security. by developing the use of renewable energy sources, the eu can reduce its dependence on fossil fuels and oil imports, reduce greenhouse gas emissions and stimulate economic activity in rural areas by creating new jobs and contributing to the development of agricultural land. unfortunately, in many member states, legal barriers such as the lack of promotional campaigns, the lack of a long-term fiscal policy on excise duty exemptions for bio-components, the lack of access to co-financing for investments related to the production of biodiesel and bioethanol are hampering the development of the biofuels market. therefore, simplification of the procedures promoting the cultivation of agricultural raw materials for the production of bio-components should be considered. an important element in the process of creating favourable conditions for the development of the biofuels market is the further development of support mechanisms, including a system of rebates and excise duty exemptions, which take into account the real costs of producing bio-components and biofuels.

the commission's vice-president mr president, i have listened carefully to the various comments which charlie mccreevy, the commissioner responsible for the internal market, will no doubt read carefully. it should be remembered that the commission proposed signing the hague convention because it considered it to be a good solution and that the convention was intended to clarify the applicable law, nothing more. the commission considers that investors can open an account in the united states today and that us law applies there too. the convention does not change much in this respect, because the freedom to choose the place of the accounts already exists today, even if, for some of you, the convention represents a step forward in this respect. however, mr president, after listening to the various speakers, i would like to say that the commission does not intend to remain deaf to these remarks. this debate shows that the convention is still a matter of serious concern. the commission will therefore remain open to any suggestions on this technically complex matter, which is currently blocked before the council, despite the initial support of all member states for the content of the 2002 hague convention. that's all i could add. the commission will of course be happy to work with the council and parliament to find a solution to the problem of establishing a legal framework, the risks of which we are also aware. if necessary, we will respond in person to mitigate the negative effects of the solution chosen.
